title: Fake images made to show Trump with Black supporters highlight concerns around AI and elections
text:
Fake images made to show Trump with Black supporters highlight concerns around AI and elections
Fake images of Donald Trump surrounded by smiling Black voters are circulating online, highlighting the potential dangers posed by artificial intelligence ahead of the 2024 election
WASHINGTON -- At first glance, images circulating online showing former President Donald Trump surrounded by groups of Black people smiling and laughing seem nothing out of the ordinary, but a look closer is telling.
Odd lighting and too-perfect details provide clues to the fact they were all generated using artificial intelligence. The photos, which have not been linked to the Trump campaign, emerged as Trump seeks to win over Black voters who polls show remain loyal to President Joe Biden.
The fabricated images, highlighted in a recent BBC investigation, provide further evidence to support warnings that the use of AI-generated imagery will only increase as the November general election approaches. Experts said they highlight the danger that any group — Latinos, women, older male voters — could be targeted with lifelike images meant to mislead and confuse as well as demonstrate the need for regulation around the technology.
In a report published this week, researchers at the nonprofit Center for Countering Digital Hate used several popular AI programs to show how easy it is to create realistic deepfakes that can fool voters. The researchers were able to generate images of Trump meeting with Russian operatives, Biden stuffing a ballot box and armed militia members at polling places, even though many of these AI programs say they have rules to prohibit this kind of content.
The center analyzed some of the recent deepfakes of Trump and Black voters and determined that at least one was originally created as satire but was now being shared by Trump supporters as evidence of his support among Blacks.
Social media platforms and AI companies must do more to protect users from AI’s harmful effects, said Imran Ahmed, the center’s CEO and founder.
“If a picture is worth a thousand words, then these dangerously susceptible image generators, coupled with the dismal content moderation efforts of mainstream social media, represent as powerful a tool for bad actors to mislead voters as we’ve ever seen,” Ahmed said. “This is a wake-up call for AI companies, social media platforms and lawmakers – act now or put American democracy at risk.”
The images prompted alarm on both the right and left that they could mislead people about the former president’s support among African Americans. Some in Trump’s orbit have expressed frustration at the circulation of the fake images, believing that the manufactured scenes undermine Republican outreach to Black voters.
“If you see a photo of Trump with Black folks and you don’t see it posted on an official campaign or surrogate page, it didn’t happen,” said Diante Johnson, president of the Black Conservative Federation. “It’s nonsensical to think that the Trump campaign would have to use AI to show his Black support.”
Experts expect additional efforts to use AI-generated deepfakes to target specific voter blocs in key swing states, such as Latinos, women, Asian Americans and older conservatives, or any other demographic that a campaign hopes to attract, mislead or frighten. With dozens of countries holding elections this year, the challenges posed by deepfakes are a global issue.
In January, voters in New Hampshire received a robocall that mimicked Biden’s voice telling them, falsely, that if they cast a ballot in that state’s primary they would be ineligible to vote in the general election. A political consultant later acknowledged creating the robocall, which may be the first known attempt to use AI to interfere with a U.S. election.
Such content can have a corrosive effect even when it’s not believed, according to a February study by researchers at Stanford University examining the potential impacts of AI on Black communities. When people realize they can’t trust images they see online, they may start to discount legitimate sources of information.
“As AI-generated content becomes more prevalent and difficult to distinguish from human-generated content, individuals may become more skeptical and distrustful of the information they receive,” the researchers wrote.
Even if it doesn't succeed in fooling a large number of voters, AI-generated content about voting, candidates and elections can make it harder for anyone to distinguish fact from fiction, causing them to discount legitimate sources of information and fueling a loss of trust that’s undermining faith in democracy while widening political polarization.
While false claims about candidates and elections are nothing new, AI makes it faster, cheaper and easier than ever to craft lifelike images, video and audio. When released onto social media platforms like TikTok, Facebook or X, AI deepfakes can reach millions before tech companies, government officials or legitimate news outlets are even aware of their existence.
“AI simply accelerated and pressed fast forward on misinformation,” said Joe Paul, a business executive and advocate who has worked to increase digital access among communities of color. Paul noted that Black communities often have “this history of mistrust” with major institutions, including in politics and media, that both make Black communities more skeptical of public narratives about them as well as fact-checking meant to inform the community.
Digital literacy and critical thinking skills are one defense against AI-generated misinformation, Paul said. “The goal is to empower folks to critically evaluate the information that they encounter online. The ability to think critically is a lost art among all communities, not just Black communities.”

title: How Stitch Fix Is Using Generative AI To Help Us Dress Better
text:
Business leaders looking to harness generative AI – the technology made famous by ChatGPT – are facing some major strategic questions. What are the best ways to use generative AI within the organization? Where can the technology add the most value? And how can you find a delicate balance between human expertise and machine intelligence?
Online personal styling service Stitch Fix is a business that all organizations can learn from. The company was built on data and AI from the ground up, allowing it to provide a personalized styling service and ship clothes directly to customers’ doors – clothes that they know clients will love based on their style preferences and previous choices. But what makes Stitch Fix really special is its ability to strike that perfect balance between human knowledge and machine capabilities. Here’s how Stitch Fix is harnessing generative AI to streamline processes and provide a better service to customers.
A Data Goldmine
Stitch Fix is sitting on a goldmine of nearly 4.5 billion text data points that clients have shared with the company. This data may include a client's style preferences or feedback on how an item fits them, for instance. It's valuable data for understanding each customer’s style, but it’s often in the form of freeform text – making it tricky data to work with. Generative AI helps Stitch Fix leverage this complex, messy data because generative AI excels at quickly making sense of and summarizing vast amounts of text data.
Stitch Fix uses large language models from OpenAI, combined with their own deep learning recommendation algorithms, to interpret the feedback that clients share and then use that information to inform future recommendations. In other words, generative AI translates customer feedback into a format that Stitch Fix recommendation algorithms can understand more easily.
Let’s explore some specific use cases in a little more detail.
Creating Clothing Recommendations
One of the ways Stitch Fix uses generative AI is to surface a selection of clothing items based on feedback the client has shared about their style preferences and fit. These recommendations are shared with a human stylist, who will then curate the final pieces for the individual client.
Considering Stitch Fix has thousands of pieces in its inventory, this initial recommendation saves stylists valuable time and allows them to spend more time focusing on the client's personal style needs.
Supporting Text Generation
Generative AI isn’t just about interpreting text. It can also create text (and images, and video, and more). Stitch Fix uses this ability to produce engaging ad copy that communicates the benefits of signing up for Stitch Fix’s service. All copy generated by AI is quality checked by human copywriters (with a 77 percent pass rate at the time of writing).
Generative AI also helps Stitch Fix create informative product descriptions that give clients details about an item’s features, specifications, and benefits. Writing descriptions for thousands of items is, as you can imagine, a time-consuming task. But having trained OpenAI’s GPT-3 on previous product descriptions (written by copywriters), plus feedback from clients, the model can now quickly create descriptions for copywriters and merchandisers to review. Stitch Fix says the model can generate 10,000 product descriptions every 30 minutes, with each description only needing a quick one-minute review by an expert before approval.
Automatically Styling Outfits
Another interesting use is Stitch Fix’s Outfit Creation Model (OCM), which uses generative AI to generate millions of new outfit combinations per day. OCM, which was trained on millions of outfits created by stylists, picks items from Stitch Fix’s current inventory, as well as from customers’ previous purchases, to compile personalized outfit suggestions for clients. This shows clients how to style items they might be interested in purchasing (or already own) with other items available from Stitch Fix. This is done through personalized emails and ads and through the customer’s personalized shopping feed.
Key Takeaways
In short, Stitch Fix uses generative AI to better understand what customers want – and, importantly, to strike a balance between automation and human skills. By letting AI systems automate the time-consuming, repetitive tasks, Stitch Fix frees up human experts to focus on their uniquely human capabilities like creativity, judgment, and building awesome relationships with clients. This is why I think all organizations can learn from Stitch Fix's approach.

title: How To Upscale AI Images For Poster-Sized Prints
text:
Generative AI art services are capable of delivering mind-blowing images—artwork so good that you might want to hang it on your wall. But there’s one big problem with AI-generated images: they’re too small!
The resolution of images created by services such as ChatGPT’s DALLE or Adobe’s Firefly are often not high resolution enough to print at A4 size, let alone anything bigger.
If you want to avoid fuzzy-looking artwork, you’re going to need to upscale your images. Let’s explore the different ways to upscale AI art and how to boost your AI creations to poster-sized prints.
Free Image Upscalers
If you type “free image upscalers” into Google, you’ll find dozens of online services offering to upload and upscale your images for free. However, these services often deliver mixed results and are beset with restrictions.
Upscale.media from Pixelbin.io is a good example. It did a passable job of upscaling an AI-generated image of an oak tree that I uploaded to the service, but it smeared details, it’s limited to 2x upscaling (doubling the dimensions of the image), and you can only upload images smaller than 1,500 x 1,500 pixels in the first place.
It was a similar story with imgupscaler.com. Its free service limits you to uploading JPEG or PNG files, not the WEBP files created by ChatGPT for instance. There are tight size restrictions too and the results were underwhelming.
These free services may just about deliver a result that’s usable for the web, but if you want to print your AI art creations, you’re almost certainly going to need pay for pro-grade upscaling.
Upscaling Images In Adobe Lightroom
It’s not only dedicated upscaling software that can blow up the size of your AI images, but everyday photo-editing software too. Adobe Lightroom, for instance, has a tucked away feature that can upscale low-resolution images.
To access the “super resolution” feature in Adobe Lightroom Classic:
- Right-click on any image in your Adobe Lightroom library
- Select Enhance
- Ensure the Super resolution box is ticked in the window that appears
You don’t get too many controls to play with, but Lightroom did a decent job of doubling the dimensions of a moody seascape I created with Midjourney.
If you’re looking at the preview image above and thinking that looks shocking, bear in mind that it’s at full zoom. Although Lightroom’s upscaled image does contain some noisy artefacts, it did a very decent job of doubling the size of the AI art.
However, if you want the best results and greater control over the upscaling process, you’re going to need dedicated upscaling software.
Upscaling Images With Topaz Gigapixel 7
If you’re regularly upscaling AI art or any other type of image, it’s worth investing in dedicated software. Topaz Gigapixel 7 certainly isn’t cheap at $99, but it’s a pro-grade tool that delivers high-quality results.
Gigapixel 7 has a range of AI models that you can choose from to get the best results. It has a model dedicated to AI-generated art, for example, one suited to buildings and architecture, another for very low-resolution images, and more.
It also gives you full control over the degree of upscaling you require. There are presets for 2x, 4x and 6x, or you can set a specific width/height if there are minimum size requirements you have to meet.
In all my tests, using both real photos and AI-generated art, Gigapixel 7 has delivered impressive results with low levels of noise and blur (both of which can be controlled with sliders, by the way).
Its real strength is “retaining” detail. I fed it an already reasonably high-resolution 2,912 × 1,632 image from Midjourney and processed a 4x upscale. Within a few seconds on my MacBook Pro, it delivered a whopping 11,648 × 6,528 image that showed almost no sign of artificial enhancement, with details such as individual whiskers in a man’s beard still looking perfectly sharp.
If you want to view the full-resolution upscaled image and see for yourself, you can download the original and upscaled images here.
I used the word retaining in quote marks above because, of course, there is no detail to retain when you’re upscaling images. The AI model is effectively adding detail to the image by best guessing what it should like.
“Just purely mathematically, if you have a photo and you 4x upscale the photo, then you have 16x more pixels,” said Eric Yang, CEO of Topaz Labs, in a briefing with me this week. “So then 15 out of those 16 pixels would be generated.”
However, what we’re talking about here is educated guesswork, not complete invention. The Topaz Gigapixel AI “will use a lot of the surrounding context in order to generate it, so it won't copy and paste things in from another image.”
Yang insists that Gigapixel AI has no more trouble upscaling AI-generated images than it does real photos. And there’s a growing trend for people wanting to print AI-generated images at size. “A huge use case of Gigapixel is preparing images for print,” he said.
“Print sounds like a kind of old-school use case. We're actually seeing that more and more people are doing it as it becomes easier to generate content. And, of course, print requires extremely high resolution and high quality, and AI upscaling is a fantastic match for that.”
And unlike in real photos, where AI might invent the detail of someone’s face that doesn’t actually look like the real person, that’s of lesser concern with AI-generated images, where faces are faked in the first place.
The final advantage of using local software such as Gigapixel AI—which is available for Mac and Windows—is that you’re not at the mercy of online services, which normally charge based on usage and often have opaque privacy policies. The AI models are downloaded to your computer, so you can upscale as many images as you like and neither the source nor upscaled images ever leave your system, unless you decide to share them.

title: Council Post: Generative AI: Pioneering A New Era In Market Dynamics And Content Creation
text:
Founder and CEO of Akool.
In the evolving landscape of technology, generative AI stands at the forefront of innovation. As a generative AI expert with over 10 years of experience, including researching, publishing on the topic and implementing AI initiatives at large companies, I’ve seen how this technology is redefining the paradigms of automation and creative expression.
This advanced technology not only is revolutionizing the approach to routine tasks but also is reshaping the creative processes in various market sectors, particularly in marketing. Its applications span a broad spectrum, heralding a new era in how businesses engage with customers and create compelling marketing content.
How Generative AI Works
Generative AI, a powerful branch of artificial intelligence, is designed to create new and original content by analyzing extensive datasets. This form of AI transcends traditional data analysis and decision making; it is adept at generating text, images, videos and even complex coding structures, paralleling human creativity.
Utilizing advanced deep learning models, such as neural networks, generative AI can discern patterns, styles and structures in data, enabling the production of unique and high-quality content. This capability marks a significant milestone, bridging the gap between algorithmic precision and artistic creativity.
The Market Impact
The market impact of generative AI is vast and transformative. Key industries like marketing, entertainment and software development already embracing this technology.
In marketing, generative AI is changing how businesses communicate with their audience. AI-driven marketing campaigns can produce personalized content, tailoring messages to specific demographics, from product recommendations to personalized shopping experiences. This not only boosts customer engagement but also optimizes marketing resources by targeting the right audience effectively.
Furthermore, generative AI is transforming visual content creation. It can design eye-catching graphics, logos and even video content, tailored to specific branding requirements and aesthetic preferences. These AI-generated visuals offer a level of creativity and customization that was previously unattainable at scale. For example, marketers can generate high resolution images for marketing collateral within seconds, bypassing a lengthy digital editing process.
In today’s globalized market, leveraging video translation for product endorsements is another strategic move for brands aiming to tap into new demographics. For example, in a scenario where a popular celebrity is featured in an endorsement video, previously the message was limited to a specific region. With AI, the video can undergo a sophisticated translation process. This includes subtitled and dubbed versions that accurately convey the celebrity’s message and maintain their engaging demeanor.
Best Practices For Working With Generative AI
A good starting point involves setting clear objectives for what you hope to achieve, such as increased customer engagement or more efficient content production. This focus helps tailor your AI strategies and measure their success accurately.
Moreover, treat AI as an enhancement to your team’s creativity, not a replacement. While AI can provide new insights and streamline processes, the unique human touch remains invaluable.
When using generative AI for creating faceswaps, art, images or marketing collateral, businesses might encounter specific challenges such as unrealistic expectations and creative limitations. One common mistake is expecting AI to perfectly understand and execute complex creative visions without significant input or guidance. This can lead to outcomes that don’t fully align with the brand’s identity or the intended message, causing frustration and potentially off-brand content.
Another challenge is navigating the fine line between innovation and brand consistency. Generative AI can produce highly creative and unique content, but without careful oversight, this content may stray too far from established brand guidelines, confusing the audience or diluting brand identity.
As generative AI keeps evolving, I think its potential to transform marketing strategies and content creation is boundless. The synergy between human creativity and AI-driven efficiency is setting the stage for a new era of personalized and innovative marketing.

title: Council Post: The Top Five Trends Impacting Cost Engineering In 2024
text:
Dan Galorath is founder and CEO of Galorath, a leader in cost estimation, actionable data and expertise for informed decision-making.
Cost engineering has always been pivotal in balancing project aspirations with practical budgetary constraints. However, the complexity of modern projects and heightened expectations for sustainability and efficiency demands a more nuanced approach. Today's cost engineers must navigate a landscape where traditional methods intersect with cutting-edge technologies and innovative practices. Driven by technological advancements, environmental considerations and evolving project management methodologies, the landscape of cost engineering is rapidly changing.
With over 40 years of experience in engineering, software, estimating and analysis, I’ve watched the cost engineering industry evolve, adapting to economic change and innovations. In this article, I'll dive deeper into five trends poised to impact the industry's future and how cost engineers can equip themselves with the knowledge and tools to lead their projects toward success in an ever-evolving landscape.
1. Artificial Intelligence
Artificial intelligence (AI) will be increasingly pivotal in cost engineering. AI's capabilities in predictive analytics, machine learning and data processing transform how cost engineers approach project estimation and risk assessment.
Its impact is multifaceted. One key area is its ability to enhance predictive analytics. AI algorithms can analyze vast datasets to forecast potential cost overruns and identify risk factors early in the project lifecycle. This enables cost engineers to make more informed decisions, leading to more accurate and reliable project outcomes.
The opportunities presented by AI in cost engineering are too significant to ignore, yet the integration also presents challenges, one primary concern being the need for high-quality data. To overcome some obstacles, ensure your team has the suitable systems and programs to provide accurate and comprehensive data to produce reliable predictions. In addition, finding professionals skilled in cost engineering and AI technologies can help harness the latest AI tools effectively.
2. Digital Twins
These virtual replicas of physical assets, processes or systems reshape project planning and redefine project cost analysis and prediction. Over the next few years, the adoption of digital twins in cost engineering will increase significantly, with predictive maintenance expected to account for the largest size of the digital twin market through 2028.
The power of digital twins lies in their ability to simulate various scenarios. This allows for early identification of cost overruns and inefficiencies while enabling organizations to test the impact of changes in a virtual environment. Real-time data is another significant advantage. This continuous stream of information is crucial for monitoring project progress and costs, enabling timely adjustments and optimizations. It also supports a continuous improvement approach. Initial investment and the need for specialized skills are significant factors leaders must consider; however, when necessary steps are taken—such as proper employee training and access to vast historical data—the opportunities presented by digital twins are too substantial to overlook.
3. Leveraging Data-Driven Decision-Making
2024 will mark a significant leap in adopting data-driven decision-making in cost engineering. Gartner estimates that by 2026, 65% of B2B sales organizations will transition from intuition-based to data-driven decision-making, using technology that unites workflow, data and analytics. Fueled by advanced analytics tools and increasing digitization of project data, data-driven decision-making enables cost engineers to move beyond traditional, antiquated estimation methods for more precise and dynamic models that adapt to changing project conditions. For example, predictive analytics can forecast potential cost overruns and suggest corrective actions, while real-time data monitoring can provide ongoing insights into project performance.
Data-driven decision-making can ensure more accurate, efficient and transparent project outcomes. However, effectively integrating these tools into existing workflows can take time and effort. Cost engineers must be proficient in data analysis and interpreting and communicating these insights to stakeholders.
4. Advanced Risk Analysis And Management Techniques
The complexity and scale of modern projects demand a more advanced approach to identifying, analyzing and mitigating risks. Integrating advanced risk management techniques is crucial for the success of projects.
Organizations need to approach risk management proactively rather than reactively. This involves using predictive analytics to foresee potential issues before they become problematic. Several tools are becoming more prevalent, allowing cost engineers to model various risk scenarios and their potential impact on project costs and timelines. However, the challenge lies in the need for continuous monitoring and updating of risk assessments.
As the founder and CEO of a company dedicated to alleviating such challenges, I understand the value of these tools. However, the benefits can only be noticed with the right resources and support to ensure seamless workflow integration. Leaders should seek out cost engineering technology that is accompanied by services such as consulting, training and support to ensure their teams get the most out of the tools and ability to address real-life situations.
5. Sustainable And Green Engineering
Environmentally sustainable practices are a fundamental shift in project planning and execution. The focus increases on incorporating sustainable materials and technologies, driven by growing awareness of environmental impacts and the long-term benefits of eco-friendly choices.
Data-driven decision-making is crucial for evaluating the cost implications of sustainable options. By employing should-cost analysis, cost engineers can balance environmental responsibility with financial viability, ensuring sustainable solutions are beneficial for the planet and economically sound. According to the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA), sustainable engineering practices minimize environmental impact and lead to substantial cost savings in the long run. This is particularly relevant in sectors like construction and manufacturing, where material choices and process efficiencies play a significant role in environmental and financial outcomes.
It’s not just about being environmentally conscious; it's about redefining cost efficiency to align financial goals with the broader objectives of sustainability and social responsibility.
Conclusion
The field of cost engineering is on the brink of change, marked by groundbreaking trends that promise to redefine the landscape of project planning and execution. The professionals who embrace these trends, equip themselves with the necessary tools and knowledge, and adopt a forward-thinking approach will lead their projects toward success.

title: Council Post: How Leaders Can Use AI To Create Great Workplace Experiences
text:
Hugo Sarrazin is the chief product and technology officer at UKG, where he designs technology experiences that support great places to work.
There’s a lot of scrutiny around artificial intelligence (AI)—the ability of software to mimic human behavior—but we are also potentially facing a once-in-a-generation opportunity to support people everywhere, particularly front-line workers, in many straightforward, low-risk and meaningful ways.
We know that organizations have faced serious challenges around workforce turnover and declining worker productivity, particularly in many critical front-line industries. We know workers themselves are expressing frustration with the status quo, which also shows up in shrinking workforce participation and increasing labor union activities.
One thing that makes a difference to workers is trust. This holds in the application and adoption of AI: A recent UKG study with more than 4,000 workers worldwide showed that 3 out of 4 (75%) would be more accepting and excited about AI if their companies were more transparent about their plans and if they understood the direct ways AI could improve their workflows (78%).
Trust comes through transparency and flexibility—being clear about where and why an organization is doing something and empowering individuals to determine what works best for them. A new research article in Harvard Business Review shows the companies most successful in adopting AI trust their employees to experiment with it and figure out how to best augment their own tasks. Leaders “can set broad objectives such as increasing accuracy or doing a particular task faster, but they should allow employees to experiment to determine how best to segment their work.”
The key to success then to developing and deploying AI in the workplace may include:
• Predictive machine learning (ML) applications like recommendations and suggestions.
• Generative or large natural language processing models (LLMs) that can retrieve, summarize and author texts.
• Conversational or natural language interactions that can understand peoples’ intents and context in ongoing exchanges.
From a digital systems perspective, AI can make all the moments that matter to workers, big and small, much more intuitive to execute, compelling to adopt and efficient to use.
This day-to-day approach is exponentially more powerful and important because we know that what employees need and care about at work varies greatly by industry, role and even time of day—as well as by many demographic and situational factors. Every person is different.
Principles Of AI Use
So to improve everyday individual worker system interactions and experiences at scale is difficult if not impossible without AI. By being able to apply large data and language processing capabilities learned from the public internet to enterprise-grade and quantities of data under proper privacy and security, leaders can leverage AI to beneficially impact workforce productivity and employee experience with little ethical, privacy or copyright risks through three principles.
• Each employee’s needs are unique, so you can use AI to offer personalization in digital systems instead of wasting workers’ time trying to find information and how to execute transactions. Arguably too much technology proliferation has impacted productivity, and AI can be used to simplify things for people—giving them faster and better access to data and capabilities they already are entitled to across disparate systems. This includes just-in-time information on how to use the systems themselves, which for many front-line workers is not from behind traditional desks or laptop computers. For example, can a retailer use AI to recommend to employees what open shifts to take or co-workers to swap with based on a real-time understanding of both shoppers’ and employees’ needs?
• Every employee’s experience is different, so AI can be applied to support flexibility in helping workers achieve personal needs and wants. Again, through adapting nearly infinite combinations of work and workplace preferences within parameters that work for both employer and employee, AI ends one-size-fits-all all functionality and features that undermine equity and fairness. Giving managers just-in-time natural language guidance on best practices on how to support the disparate needs of a diverse workforce is also a key flexibility concept. For example, as a manager is about to have an interaction with a worker, can he or she dynamically be coached or given a script that matches what an individual employee wants and needs from the job from best practice texts that build trust?
• To show and maintain confidence in a trusting employer/employee relationship, AI can facilitate transparency in many ways and organizational areas, again by targeting and democratizing information sharing and visibility. This will be particularly true around how AI itself is deployed—as overt and explainable as possible—and never replacing human decision-making responsibilities. For example, visually flagging wherever AI is making recommendations or suggestions in a system with easy-to-understand explanations of both the users’ responsibilities in decision-making and the benefits of the AI-driven feature.
In these ways, leaders can use AI to give workers time back, which can positively affect productivity on the job as well as help meet their personal preferences. The latest advancements in AI offer all workers learning and development in new ways of working digitally alongside algorithmic capabilities and potentially opening brand-new career paths for people. Because the outcome for applying any kind of new technology shouldn’t just be tactical or incremental improvements in productivity but to support broader and bolder business outcomes. Showing employees respect by offering personalized professional support, transparency of information, and empowerment in making decisions are key enablers of building a culture of trust that underpins a great place to work. It’s time to consider how organizations can embrace and apply the latest generation of AI technologies to this practical yet profound outcome.

title: Up 12% This Year On AI Tailwinds, Will Micron Stock See Further Gains Following Q2 Results?
text:
Micron Technology (NASDAQ: MU) is expected to publish its Q2 2024 results around March 20, reporting on a quarter that is likely to see the company benefit from stronger pricing for DRAM memory and higher demand for High Bandwidth Memory targeted at AI applications. Micron has guided for revenues of between $5.1 billion to $5.5 billion, marking an increase of about 42% versus the last year, while projecting an adjusted net loss of $0.28 per share, at the mid-point. So what are some of the trends that are likely to drive Micron’s earnings for the quarter?
Memory prices have been trending higher, driven by a slew of factors. Firstly, memory majors including Micron and Samsung have pared back on their investment in memory capacity and have been rationalizing their production in recent months and this has been helping prices. Moreover, the memory market is also seeing demand from the replenishment of memory inventory by smartphone OEMs. The PC market is also seeing a rebound. According to research firm Canalys, PC shipments are likely to approach 267 million in 2024, marking an increase of 8% from 2023. Moreover, the advent of generative AI tools such as the popular ChatGPT is also likely to drive up memory demand since these algorithms typically require more storage and DRAM resources compared to other types of algorithms. AI requires high-bandwidth memory for training large language models and inferencing quickly, and Micron has not been typically viewed as a leader in this space. However, the company recently announced the specifications for its latest HBM3 second-generation memory which is considerably ahead of its rivals, with shipments estimated to start in early 2024. We also expect Micron’s margins to see a slight recovery. The company has guided gross margins of between 11.5% to 14.5% for the quarter, up from just about 1% in Q1 FY’24 and -9% in Q4 FY’23.
However, the increase in MU stock has been far from consistent. Returns for the stock were 24% in 2021, -46% in 2022, and 71% in 2023. In comparison, returns for the S&P 500 have been 27% in 2021, -19% in 2022, and 24% in 2023 - indicating that MU underperformed the S&P in 2021 and 2022. In fact, consistently beating the S&P 500 - in good times and bad - has been difficult over recent years for individual stocks; for heavyweights in the Information Technology sector including MSFT, AAPL, and NVDA, and even for the megacap stars GOOG, TSLA, and AMZN. Micron has indicated that it expects a revenue hit to the tune of a low single to a high single-digit percentage. There are also concerns about the global economy, amid high interest rates and relatively stubborn inflation, which could weigh on consumer electronics sales. That being said, we think the overall recovery in the memory markets and the potential surge in demand from the generative AI trend could help to offset this in the medium term. LinkedIn says premium subscriptions bring in USD 1.7 bn
In new disclosure, LinkedIn says premium subscriptions bring in $1.7 billion. LinkedIn on Thursday for the first time disclosed sales for its premium subscription business, saying the unit hit $1.7 billion in revenue in 2023 as the company sees an uptick in adoption of new artificial intelligence tools. LinkedIn, the social network aimed at business professionals, has not broken out its full financial performance since it was acquired by Microsoft in 2016.
LinkedIn on Thursday for the first time disclosed sales for its premium subscription business, saying the unit hit $1.7 billion in revenue in 2023 as the company sees an uptick in adoption of new artificial intelligence tools.
LinkedIn, the social network aimed at business professionals, has not broken out its full financial performance since it was acquired by Microsoft in 2016. The company has previously disclosed that it made $15 billion in fiscal 2023, with $7 billion of that coming from hiring software that it sells to corporate recruiters.
But over the past year, LinkedIn has been working to expand its premium subscription business, which is used by job seekers and other individual users and starts at $39.99 per month.
A major part of that effort was the addition last year of AI features such as the ability to scan a job posting and, based on a job seeker's resume, automatically determine if the seeker might be a good fit. The AI system can also help job seekers tweak their LinkedIn profile to make them more appealing to recruiters and can automatically generate written messages to send to recruiters.
In an interview, Dan Shapero, LinkedIn's chief operating officer, said the number of LinkedIn premium subscribers rose 25% in 2023, though the company did not give an absolute figure.
Shapero said that LinkedIn's early data shows that 70% of subscribers with access to the new AI tools have tried them, and 90% of those found them useful. While the labor market remains tight in the U.S., that dynamic is uneven across industries and LinkedIn data shows there are still two applicants for every job.
"What we do know is that because of the uncertainty in the broader economy, there are people that are trying to make sure that they have the ability to get the best job that they can and that they're excited about," Shapero said.

title: Council Post: Renewing Corporate Gifting: The Impact Of AI On Personalization
text:
Archer Chiang, Founder/CEO at Giftpack.
The corporate gifting landscape has grappled with the challenges of personalization in traditional and scalable employee recognition methods for a long time. But artificial intelligence is already making an impact on corporate gifting, addressing inherent issues in manufacturing and distribution, and it continues unlocking possibilities for the future of corporate gifting.
The Corporate Gifting Landscape
Thoughtful gifts can enhance client loyalty and satisfaction. According to a recent survey, 80% of corporate gift buyers say gifting has improved their relationships with clients.
Personalization is a cornerstone in effective corporate gifting, offering a tailored experience that resonates with the recipient. The level of personalization serves not only as a gesture of goodwill but also as a strategic approach to strengthen business relationships and partnerships.
However, in an era with remote work and increasing cross-border sales through e-commerce, creating personal connections to clients and sales leads can be more difficult than ever. According to Elizabeth Dunn, a psychology professor, “Choosing the wrong gift can be kind of risky for relationships because it says you don’t have anything in common.” This can have a big impact on a company’s ability to develop strong personal relationships that generate sales and create strong relationships with clients.
Challenges In Traditional Gift Personalization Manufacturing
Manual personalization processes have long posed challenges in the corporate gifting landscape. Traditional methods often struggle to meet scalability demands, resulting in generic and uninspired gifts.
Two seemingly minor obstacles are actually the root cause of the struggle: Firstly, platforms often struggle to adequately display gift images, leading to recipients receiving items that may not align with their expectations. Secondly, the production of personalized designs demands a significant investment in human resources for design, manufacturing, sourcing and distribution needs.
This limitation has prompted many businesses to seek innovative solutions to redefine their gifting strategies. According to my company’s research in June 2023, 70% of people feel that personalizing gifts is a challenge. Budgeting, logistics and a lack of understanding about the gift recipient are the most common challenges businesses are facing. Our research involved 43 mid to large enterprises, with a diverse participant pool representative of various industries and organizational scales, and approximately 250 individuals contributed their insights.
AI In Gift Personalization: A Game-Changer
I think artificial intelligence will revolutionize gift personalization. In fact, this technological shift has already started, as companies like mine and others in the industry embrace AI for gifting. This signifies a pivotal moment in redefining how businesses are investing in technology that helps express appreciation, build relationships and contribute to a thriving corporate culture.
AI algorithms and machine learning capabilities empower businesses to enhance personalization processes at scale and across geographic divides. It can source and recommend gifts based on recipient preferences, automate the ordering and delivery process, and also help with customizing and manufacturing personalized gifts at scale.
The power of AI lies in its capacity to analyze vast datasets, enabling businesses to understand the individual preferences of their colleagues and tailor gifts accordingly. With AI, this can be done in the matter of a few seconds. Encouraging businesses to embrace AI solutions can help them overcome the constraints associated with traditional, at scale gift personalization methods.
While AI gifting offers significant advantages, it isn’t without its challenges. A primary concern is the potential for impersonalization, as algorithms may overlook individual preferences. Data privacy is another hurdle, as AI systems require access to personal information for tailored recommendations. Balancing customization with privacy is crucial.
To overcome these challenges, businesses should continually refine AI algorithms or consider tools that do so—treating AI as a helpful aid rather than completely relying on it. For data privacy and security, businesses should focus on building robust privacy protocols and transparent communication—ensuring recipients know their personal information is always secure. In overcoming these challenges, AI gifting can become even more reliable.
Best Practices For Personalizing Gifts
When personalizing gifts, business leaders should prioritize understanding recipients’ individual preferences and interests. Utilize available data, engage in conversations and pay attention to details that showcase a genuine understanding of their tastes. Incorporate the company’s values and culture for an added layer of personalization. Lastly, consider the occasion and timing to ensure the gesture is both personal and timely.
For those using AI gifting solutions, balance automation and personalization by continually refining algorithms based on user feedback. Prioritize robust privacy protocols and transparent communication about data usage to build trust. Treat AI as a supportive tool rather than depending on it completely, preserving the human touch in the gifting process. Automate everything from data collection to gift delivery, but pay extra attention to AI recommended gifts to ensure accuracy of personalization.
For those unable to leverage AI gifting solutions, you can still personalize gifts by truly understanding the recipient’s preferences through conversations or shared experiences. Use of handwritten notes and customized packaging elevate the personalized experience. Consider timing and appropriateness to ensure the gift resonates effectively, as the essence of personalization lies in the sincerity and thoughtfulness behind each gesture. Although it may take you a longer time, personalized gifting is still very much doable without AI.
Anticipating future advancements in gift personalization, I envision a landscape where AI-driven solutions provide increasingly sophisticated and personalized experiences. The role of AI in shaping the future of corporate culture is significant, as businesses must invest in technology that creates meaningful connections between colleagues at work.

title: Council Post: The Rise Of Open Artificial Intelligence: Open-Source Best Practices
text:
Tyler Weitzman, cofounder, President and Head of AI at Speechify.
Every day, open-source AI technology powers more and more models. The 2023 “Open Source Security and RiskAnalysis” report by Synopsys found that 76% of code scanned in codebases was open source. In artificial intelligence, with an ecosystem dependent on public research and baseline dependencies, I believe the percentage is likely even higher.
A few months ago, a software engineer at Google released a document on a public Discord server. He said the "gap is closing" in terms of the edge Google and OpenAI have on open-source technology. The document states, “We (Google) have no moat, and neither does OpenAI.”
According to the leaked document, the engineer thinks open-source AI will outclass Google and OpenAI because the open-source community has now solved the “major open problems” and made it accessible to the general public. OpenAI’s and Google’s models are still better in quality, the document said, but "open-source models are faster, more customizable, more private, and pound-for-pound more capable."
At my company, we have combined closed-source AI research with open-source language and audio models to create text-to-speech tools for users, and this experience has shown me the capabilities of open-source AI in today's fast-paced digital landscape.
Benefits And Risks Of Open-Source AI
In the early days, implementing large language models was considered an expensive approach to driving research and innovation. But today, open-sourced LLMs can provide benefits for businesses with little implementation investment. Here are some of the benefits of open-source LLMs versus paying for third-party APIs:
• Security: Integrating LLMs into their own infrastructure can give companies control over their data and secure their sensitive information, whether on-premises or in the cloud. This can help prevent unauthorized access and data leaks.
• Transparency: An open-source LLM also gives companies transparency about their working mechanism, data training and architecture. This can make it easier to understand the shortcomings and biases of the model, as well as the tasks in which it may specialize.
• Price: In my experience, open-source LLMs are typically less expensive than proprietary LLMs, as they primarily involve hosting fees rather than margins and licensing fees to the developer. There are a variety of sizes of models available with a range of open-source performance optimizations to lower cost.
• Customizable: Pretrained open-source LLMs are easily tunable and customizable. Businesses can specialize these models to specific datasets and benefit from free community development support for any issues encountered.
However, businesses should also consider some shortcomings of self-hosting open-source AI before using or offering this technology. Open-source software often requires more time invested than paying an API provider, and community support is not being paid to solve every issue for you, so users have to debug and search for answers on online forums. Some tools might also not be as user-friendly, which can limit their usage to only experienced developers or data scientists.
I've found that many open-source AI solutions also lack quality assurance and testing, which can lead to sudden bugs or instability. There can also be security concerns, and there’s a need to validate that the repository has the appropriate licenses for a company’s intended use. I’d recommend organizations address and plan proactively for these challenges.
Organizations Releasing Open-Source Models
Considering the rising popularity of open-source models, many growing startups and bigger corporations, such as Meta, have included open-source AI in their strategy-making. Some examples of open-source models include:
• Llama 2: Owned by Meta, Llama 2 consists of pretrained LLMs with up to 70 billion parameters. It is a licensed open-source LLM for commercial use.
• Vicuna and Alpaca: These models were developed on top of Llama to be GPT-4-level language models.
• Falcon: The Falcon LLM is the Technology Innovation Institute's open-source model that can be used for research or commercial use.
• Bloom: BigScience released Bloom, a multilingual language model built by 1,000-plus researchers.
• MPT-7B and MPT-30B: Databricks acquired MosaicML, an open-source startup that developed MPT-7B and MPT-30B.
• Mistral 7B and Mixtral 8x7B: Mistral AI, a French startup, released Mistral 7B, a 7.3 billion parameter model that surpassed larger models in benchmarks, and Mixtral 8x7B, a 46.7 billion parameter model that uses a mixture of experts architecture. Both are under the Apache 2.0 license for open use.
Some other open-source models include Google's FLAN-T5, GitHub and Hugging Face’s StarCoder, Together AI’s RedPajama-INCITE-3B and Cerebras’ Cerebras-GPT. These models are trained on modern AI algorithms and help companies become a part of the open-source community.
Why did Meta open-source Llama? According to a blog by the company, titled "Introducing LLaMA: A foundational, 65-billion-parameter large language model," open-sourcing Llama would help further democratize access for those who don't otherwise have access. In other cases, companies might open-source to attract customers and developers. I believe OpenAI, for example, built much of its initial branding off of open-sourcing the earlier versions of its GPT systems.
Meanwhile, I've found that many individual developers believe enough in the mission of democratized AI that they contribute to open-source voluntarily and at no charge. Companies that open-source can benefit from contributions from this community of developers.
Getting Started With Open-Source AI
The future seems promising for the open-source community, and, from my view, it won’t take much longer for this technology to catch up to large organizations. Thus, I believe participating in part of this ecosystem will position businesses to thrive in the market.
It is also important to address the security, usability and stability concerns surrounding open-source AI. Today, I find that people want little to no restrictions when using LLMs. Corporations will need to take some necessary steps to establish themselves as leaders in the open-source community while safe-guarding against abuse.
Companies should also ensure effective governance around open-source models with robust legal frameworks that mitigate threats. Implementing these strategies can help businesses set themselves up for success in the open-source AI ecosystem.

text:
Gavin McMahon is a founder and CEO of fassforward, specializing in storytelling, leadership and business transformation.
In science fiction, AI is often portrayed as a menacing force, from HAL 9000's refusal to open the pod bay doors in "2001: A Space Odyssey" to the time-traveling T-800's mission to eliminate Sarah Connor in "The Terminator." These stories serve as cautionary tales about the perils of humans granting machines the power to think.
Now, science fiction is science fact, and the real-world impact of AI is proving to be more nuanced and more profound. Tom Wilson, the CEO of Allstate, predicts it will hit the economy "like a tsunami." The head of the IMF predicts (download required) that “AI adoption may destroy some jobs (and displace the associated workers) and create or enhance others.” And according to IBM Chairman and CEO Arvind Krishna, "If the lower half of cognitive work gets taken over by genAI, it implies that you've got to learn critical thinking. That means critical thinking, regardless of which domain you're in, becomes the skill that is far, far more needed."
In short: We need to get ready.
What skills can help you adapt to the AI revolution?
Based on my company's experience integrating AI into our work, I believe the following skills will be invaluable to business leaders and professionals in navigating the transition to an AI-powered economy.
• Critical And Strategic Thinking
If AI can provide you with an answer, the trick then comes in asking the right question. Enter critical thinking. With AI taking the legwork out of work, critical thinking allows you to ask the right questions, and strategic thinking helps you put those answers into a business context.
• Experience And Judgment
AI can hallucinate. It can give you nonsense, and it can also give you gems. Sifting out the wheat from the chaff requires experience and judgment. Your role, seasoned by years of experience, is to discern which AI-generated ideas are truly valuable. The experience of you and your team should act as a critical filter, ensuring that AI's efficiency is coupled with human wisdom and ethics so as to steer you toward relevant and practical outcomes.
• Effective Communication
AI can produce a lot of information very quickly. But that’s not going to help when we’re already drowning in data. I believe the human skills of decluttering, picking up on nuance and knowing when to speak and when to shut up will be even more valuable. Even in an AI-driven world, the ability of professionals to communicate complex ideas simply and effectively will be needed to drive collaboration, innovation and understanding across all levels of an organization.
• Leadership In A Digital Era
We are at the beginning of uncharted waters with AI. Change is coming, and it will likely feel threatening. Navigating those waters and bringing people through change requires leadership. Your role is to inspire and align your crew with the vision of your organization, transforming AI’s analytical power into strategies that resonate on a human level. Effective leadership in the AI age is about inspiring confidence and guiding teams through technological change, ensuring that AI is used ethically and aligns with your organization's values and goals.
• Curiosity And Innovation
To unlock AI’s full potential, constantly ask "what if?" and "why not?"—exploring new applications and improvements. We don’t know (yet) what AI can do to change how we run and operate as a business, but we do know it will. Treat AI as a sandbox where your curiosity builds, tests and learns. In my experience, curiosity can fuel innovation and adaptation in the AI era, driving the exploration and practical application of AI in ways that may revolutionize industries and create new opportunities.
• Proficiency In Prompt Engineering
Perhaps the most obvious of the skills is the newest: prompt engineering. The good news is, you can learn it in a weekend. The bad news: What you learn will be different from weekend to weekend. This skill isn’t coding; it’s the art and science of human-AI conversation, crafting prompts that unlock AI’s potential and make it work for you. Proficiency in prompt engineering is an important bridge between human intent and AI capability, and it can help you ensure that AI tools are effectively and accurately used to solve real-world problems and generate innovative solutions.
AI need not be the villainous force depicted in science fiction. It is a transformative technology already reshaping our world. That is why I believe that understanding and harnessing its potential will be crucial to our future.

title: Council Post: Revolutionizing Agriculture: Cost-Effective Workforce Strategies For The Modern Farm
text:
Dr. Malcolm Adams, Founder-CEO, Avid Solutions International.
In the evolving landscape of the agricultural industry, managing labor costs while ensuring a skilled and efficient workforce is a significant challenge. The integration of innovative approaches like the Workforce Innovation and Opportunity Act (WIOA) and USDA programs, along with the application of generative AI in human resources, presents a viable solution. This comprehensive strategy not only aids in financial management but also bolsters the industry’s move toward modernization and sustainability.
As a founder-CEO of a company focused on advancing food security, healthcare and labor, my journey through the realms of agritech and sustainable development has been both challenging and rewarding. My passion for leveraging technology to enhance agricultural efficiency and sustainability led me to explore innovative strategies for managing labor costs—a significant hurdle for many in our field. The desire to share practical solutions that can make a real difference for business leaders and entrepreneurs motivated me to write on this subject. My experiences, from pioneering new technologies to navigating government programs, have taught me the value of creative approaches in solving traditional industry challenges.
WIOA: A Gateway To Skilled Labor
The WIOA is a critical piece of legislation that supports workforce development across various sectors, including agriculture. A central feature of WIOA is its emphasis on registered apprenticeships. These programs are particularly relevant to the agricultural sector, offering a blend of practical on-the-job training with essential classroom learning. For agricultural businesses, this translates into a workforce trained specifically for the unique demands of the sector, ensuring that workers are not just skilled, but also aligned with the industry’s evolving needs.
These apprenticeship programs are not just about skill development; they represent a cost-effective solution for training. Businesses can leverage these programs to train new workers, significantly reducing the financial burden associated with developing a skilled workforce from scratch. Furthermore, these programs often include government subsidies or incentives, further alleviating training costs for employers.
USDA Programs: Financial Support For Innovation
The United States Department of Agriculture (USDA) plays a pivotal role in supporting the agricultural industry, particularly through its various funding and grant programs. These initiatives can provide critical financial support to farms and agricultural businesses, enabling them to invest in new technologies, improve operational efficiency and upskill their workforce.
By leveraging USDA programs, agricultural businesses can offset a significant portion of their labor costs. These programs often support initiatives that enhance sustainability and innovation in agriculture, aligning perfectly with the industry’s move toward more environmentally conscious and technologically advanced practices.
Generative AI In Human Resources: Streamlining Workforce Management
The application of generative AI in human resources is another frontier in managing labor costs effectively in agriculture. Generative AI refers to AI systems capable of producing new, valuable content based on existing data. In human resources, this technology can optimize various processes, including recruitment, training and employee management.
For example, AI-driven recruitment tools can significantly streamline the hiring process, helping agricultural businesses quickly identify the most suitable candidates for specific roles. This not only saves time but also reduces the costs associated with lengthy and often inefficient traditional recruitment processes.
Moreover, generative AI can be pivotal in developing customized training programs. These AI-driven programs can adapt to the unique learning curves and needs of each employee, ensuring efficient and effective skill development. Additionally, AI can be instrumental in employee performance management, identifying areas for improvement and providing data-driven insights for better workforce management.
Leveraging These Resources
To effectively implement these strategies, agricultural businesses need to engage in strategic planning. This involves a thorough analysis of your business’s current workforce needs, the potential benefits of WIOA and USDA programs and the applicability of generative AI in their specific context.
Businesses should evaluate how these tools and programs can be integrated into their existing operations and how they align with long-term business goals. For example, understanding the specific skills that need to be developed in their workforce and identifying the appropriate WIOA apprenticeship programs that cater to these needs is crucial. Similarly, exploring which USDA programs align with your business model and operational needs is essential.
Moreover, leaders should assess the potential of generative AI in their human resources department. This includes identifying the processes that can be optimized using AI, the type of AI technology needed and the potential return on investment.
However, implementing resources like WIOA programs and generative AI in the agricultural sector can present challenges. For instance, the use of generative AI in human resources demands a certain level of technological proficiency and an upfront investment in software and training. This learning curve can be steep for businesses not already familiar with AI applications, potentially leading to initial resistance or implementation delays.
Moreover, accessing USDA grants or taking advantage of WIOA programs often requires navigating complex application processes with specific eligibility criteria. Some businesses may find themselves disqualified due to size, location or the nature of their operations. In such cases, seeking alternative funding sources, like state or local government grants, or private sector partnerships, can be a viable path. Engaging with industry associations or hiring grant-writing experts can also enhance the chances of securing financial support for workforce development and technological upgrades.
A Holistic Approach To Labor Cost Management
By adopting a holistic approach that combines government programs like WIOA and USDA with the innovative application of generative AI in human resources, agricultural businesses can effectively manage labor costs. This strategy not only provides financial relief but also ensures the development of a skilled, efficient and future-ready workforce.
In conclusion, the agricultural industry stands at a pivotal point where the integration of these advanced strategies can significantly impact its growth and sustainability. By embracing these approaches, businesses in the sector can navigate the challenges of labor costs while investing in the long-term viability and success of their workforce and the industry.

title: Council Post: Expanding The Limits Of AI With Identity
text:
Lasse Andresen, CEO of IndyKite.
Artificial intelligence (AI) holds great promise for enterprises in all industries, with industry-specific AI models arriving as the next wave of enlightenment. However, with generative AI products trained on large quantities of data to identify patterns, the success of the model is entirely dependent on the quality, availability and validity of that input data.
Data is everywhere, but it is not always easy to interrogate the data to understand its origin, age, sensitivity and reliability. The AI surge is forcing a conversation about accessibility to this data information—especially if it is to be leveraged for AI.
Recently, this was raised by the Data & Trust Alliance as it introduced data provenance standards to enhance AI trustworthiness. The standards are designed to help companies understand where, when and how data was collected or generated to provide transparency into the rapidly growing number of AI applications.
Data provenance is a critical piece of this transparency, capturing how data flows through the organization and offering insights into data quality, security and validity. By leveraging information about the data in use, enterprises can identify and rectify potential bottlenecks, inconsistencies or inaccuracies in the data pipeline and therefore enhance the accuracy and effectiveness of the AI product. On the flip side, without data transparency, clear data provenance and data veracity indicators, it is difficult to trust the AI model and success will be hampered.
Although there are likely many ways to capture such critical information about data, I propose a novel idea. I have been working in the identity and access management (IAM) industry for a long time and founded one of the market leaders before launching my current venture, IndyKite. It is from this perspective that I believe that modern IAM is considerably underutilized in today’s tech stack, as it can offer significant benefits for AI and other modern applications, especially in terms of data veracity. Traditional IAM has been kept separate from the rest of the stack due to security concerns. However, modern IAM aims to connect disparate data silos and treat identity data as a growth enabler.
By adopting a graph-driven, modern identity approach, you can leverage a unified identity fabric, complete with context, data provenance and risk attributes for each entity (e.g., human, system, digital product or individual data points)—all without exposing sensitive data. This approach considers each application, digital entity and data point as an "identity" and captures information to support the digital trust standards described by the Data & Trust Alliance. The data can then be used in tailored AI products and automated tasks with trust while providing the necessary transparency and evidence as to its veracity.
Getting started toward greater trust in your AI-enhanced applications does not need to be an arduous process or require significant overhauling of the tech you already have in place. With the right tooling, you can leverage your data as it is, from where it is, without a huge investment. The magic is in how you approach the challenge and how you think about your data.
The best place to start is in understanding what you want your application to solve, the data you need to solve it and the veracity required of that data. A flexible data model here is vital, as it will allow you to start small and grow and change as you scale (without breaking logic or creating overly complicated data architectures). The more data mature you are, the faster this step will be.
From here you can create your unified data layer, enriched with provenance metadata and relationships. You can leverage this layer to start to drive intelligent access decisions, enhance your application logic, gain deeper data insights in your analytics or power your AI and AI-enhanced applications.
We are right at the start of seeing all that AI can offer, and I believe we are also only scraping the surface of what can be achieved with identity-centric data veracity. This next wave of AI must not just look at what AI can enable but how we can better enable AI.

title: Council Post: The Power (And Peril) Of AI In Digital Health
text:
Kal Patel, M.D., is CEO and cofounder of BrightInsight. He has over 20 years of experience in pharma, medtech and regulated digital health.
Artificial intelligence (AI) technologies are rapidly being adopted into all facets of society, and digital health is no exception. According to a Stanford University study, investment in AI systems for digital health reached nearly $29 billion from 2017 to 2021, the most of any sector. In January 2024, the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) approved its first AI-powered tool—which applies machine learning technology to mental health data—to evaluate the severity of anxiety and depression symptoms.
Here's how pharma companies that are eyeing companion apps for their therapies can leverage AI's power while mitigating its risks.
It's All About The Data
Any AI tool can only be as valuable as the data it's fed. Insights derived from data that's already being generated (for example, from office visits or lab tests) have limited value compared with insights derived from data that has never been collected before.
Successful companion apps don't take the same old data to try to solve a new problem. Instead, they create datasets such as remote infusion data or digital quality-of-life surveys that have never existed and then amplify their power with AI-generated insights.
For example, an AI-powered drug companion app could be used to predict churn by tracking metrics that it's learned are correlated with patients who are at risk of dropping the therapy.
Patient Targeting
Conversely, AI can also be used to identify patients who are least likely to churn and most likely to deliver high lifetime value. From a clinical perspective, this means the ability to target the patients who are most likely to respond well to the treatment over the long term. From a sales and marketing perspective, it's the ability to focus the effort and funding of patient recruitment on those who are most likely to remain on the therapy for its intended duration.
Driving Conversion And Adherence
Companion apps can also use AI to drive conversion to therapy by applying a set of agents to the various obstacles standing between receipt of a prescription and initiation of the actual therapy. One agent would tackle the red tape of prior authorization; another could evaluate the patient's calendar and schedule a nursing appointment to learn how to administer the therapy; another might identify the most affordable path to receiving the therapy.
AI technology can also be adapted to improve patients' adherence to therapies by maximizing the effectiveness of "nudge" reminders. One patient with rheumatoid arthritis may be motivated by the desire to play with their grandchildren, while another might be driven by anxiety over the sting and burn of injecting their medication, and a third is just so busy that they forget to take the therapy. The AI behind the app can learn what those motivations are and personalize its nudges to best suit the patient's circumstances so that they are maximally effective.
Screening For Mental Health Comorbidities
There's also a use case involving the ability to screen patients for mental health conditions, which are the most common comorbidity for almost every physical malady, carrying a global economic burden of roughly $5 trillion.
Take the rheumatoid arthritis patient who wants to be able to play with their grandchildren without pain. An AI system monitoring that patient's call to a doctor's office or insurance provider could be taught to screen for signs of depression or other mental health issues that might be affecting their therapy and quality of life.
Mental health AI-driven technology can also come in the form of a chatbot within a patient companion app that can communicate with patients in an empathetic way and deliver clinically validated care to support a patient's mental health.
Privacy, Security And Compliance
As the power of AI increases (along with the value of the data behind it), so does the importance of ensuring that the data is safely and securely stored. Making sure personal information is kept private has always been a bedrock principle in digital health, but imagine if the hacker could change the data driving real-world clinical decisions—potentially altering or even denying therapy to the patient. The stakes are higher now than ever before.
Another key consideration is bias—ensuring that the app's output is applicable to its intended patient population. App developers that operate across many disease states in many countries are well-positioned to bring in data that's representative of a wide range of patients, helping to eliminate bias.
The regulatory landscape around AI is in constant flux, both in the U.S. and abroad. A 2023 presidential executive order mandated a wide range of actions designed to address security and safety threats. The FDA also formed an advisory panel for digital health and AI in October 2023 and has issued a series of guidance documents for medical technologies that use AI.
The European Union's Artificial Intelligence Act (EU AI Act), the world's first attempt at a comprehensive, horizontal regulatory framework for AI, was endorsed by all 27 EU members. The measure, which covers both AI-enabled diagnostic and medical devices as well as AI-enabled digital health apps, is slated to be phased in over the next two years.
Companion app developers need to keep abreast of regulatory developments and make sure their products guarantee compliance across multiple jurisdictions worldwide.
Pharma and medical technology companies should consider AI through two lenses. One is internal—which areas are limited by our processes, and how can we adapt AI to ease those limitations? The second is external—which areas would benefit from a trusted partner who can leverage the technology in ways we can't?
