title: How The Telecom Industry Can Accelerate Growth From Generative AI
text:
I have been engaged in the telecommunications (”telco”) industry for over 25 years, and it is so refreshing to see the positive energy moving into this sector, as a result of applying generative AI (”gen-AI”) technologies. Gen-AI can easily analyze different types of data such as: text, images, code, voice and even create new content on demand, enabling personalization, and new customer or employee engagement experiences.
For years, growth and profitability has been a challenge requiring the telco industry to diversify and offer more professional services and seek out higher margin offerings.
Gen-AI trials are being launched, it seems everywhere, from AT&T, SK Telecom, and Vodafone. Even Bell Canada, a tier one Canadian company, according to Bell’s Director of IT Delivery, Neel Mehta is betting big on the connection between solid data foundations and an effective AI strategy. “We see data as the new oil, and AI as the refinery,” according to Gupta. Today, Bell is using a combination of generative and predictive AI to service its customers. One of Bell’s use cases is using AI to predict environmental events, such as snowstorms or heavy rains, which may cause network outages. This early risk foresight improves resourcing and workforce communication. The costs for servicing major outages of teleco providers is a heavy burden, as Rogers Communications found out last year, when more than 12 million users of its’ cable internet and cellular networks, including those of subsidiary brands Rogers Wireless, Fido, Cityfone, and Chatr were severely impacted. Using AI methods to analyze all router risk impacts and getting workforces ready for major outages is a major productivity improvement opportunity for the telco carriers.
According to IBM’s Institute for Business Value, 60% of executives will be piloting gen-AI solutions by January, 2025. What is important is that rather than taking many months to launch a pilot, gen-AI pilots can be deployed in a few weeks.
The telco industry is plagued with outdated operating practices and processes, so gen-AI is providing new profitability possibilities. In some cases, returns on incremental margins can increase 3 to 4% points in two years, and as much as 8 to 10% points in five years, by enhancing customer revenue through improved customer life cycle management and by reducing operating costs.
The industry has so much technology debt in legacy systems, that finding new pathways with gen-AI must feel like a breath of fresh. A number of use cases that can be bring more value to telco leaders include:
1.) In sales operations, capturing all the sales documentation on how to sell different products and services and pricing model information (essentially absorb all the knowing sources) can be absorbed into a powerful knowledge gen-AI engine. Other innovative sales solutions include: using a chat bot to answer any question that a sales manager or sales rep may have on a sales funnel, or bringing together real-time knowledge from the full customer experience value chain and sales practices. This may seem like a daunting opportunity, but we finally have a new suite of technology innovations where gen-AI combined with AI search and knowledge management methods will absolutely drive a winning combination to fuel increased profitability.
2.) In customer service operations, increasing agent productivity, and developing AI chatbots to improve agent support, provide promising return on investments, and are estimated to secure a 15-20% productivity impact. Another useful use case is to transcribe all voice or written client interactions into summarizations, further creating a smarter customer service knowledge center. A Latin American telco recently reported that they increased their call center agent productivity by 25% and enhanced both their customer experience, and agent skills by leveraging gen-AI recommendations.
3.) In marketing operations, gen-AI can identify new sales leads from customer calls and then target using customer micro-segments directly from the call insights. AI enables hyper-personalization, deeper customer insights, and faster content generation. A unique AI model could be developed that extracts household details, using customized marketing messages and even include customer preferences, based on cognitive learning style from persona intelligence methods, i.e.: succinct messaging, to authority messages, to storytelling messages. McKinsey recently reported that a European telco had increased their customer conversion rates for marketing campaigns by 40%, while reducing costs by using gen-AI to personalize content.
4.) In network operations, gen-AI can optimize technology configurations, enhance labor productivity, improve inventory and network planning. One large telco has accelerated their network mapping by analyzing and structuring data about network components, including specifications and maintenance information, from supplier contracts. This can enable the telco to more accurately assess component compatibility, maintenance requirements, improve operational planning and optimize capital.
What questions should Telco Board of Directors and C-Suite leaders ask to advance their AI leadership capabilities?
1.) Do we have a clearly defined AI transformation strategy and what are the cost savings opportunities to unlock unprecedented growth and new value?
2.) How good is our data and how easily accessible is it to take advantage of gen-AI?
3.) How skilled are our leaders to design, develop and sustain a gen-AI environment?
4.) Do we have the right technical infrastructure to apply gen-AI successfully?
5.) How are we ethically applying gen-AI? and
6.) How are we ensuring that we are managing our sustainability goals, given the high demands of AI on energy and water?
In summary, the telco players that are innovating and experimenting with early generative AI use cases will no doubt grow faster and capture a more significant share of the nearly $100 billion in incremental value that McKinsey is predicting. That is in addition to the $140 billion to $180 billion in productivity gains that gen-AI will create in the telco industry of what could be unlocked by traditional AI. Keeping a vigilant eye on the AI ethical impacts of sustainability and energy consumption levels is a key risk factor that the industry also must grapple with.

title: Author Post: Spring Forward With AI: Put Tech to Use for Self-Improvement
text:
March brings many things, such as the first day of spring, the vernal equinox, the time change, and the promise of warmer weather.
We know someone, or perhaps we are that person, who gets excited about the growing season of springtime. With their green thumbs up, they eagerly trudge outdoors to sow this season’s plants. Preparation is vital, whether roses and dahlias or peas and carrots.
What can we learn from these patient and persistent gardeners about artificial intelligence, which is a much more indoor activity? Let’s look at what it takes to lay down the seed of change in your personal and professional life to embrace the potential and harvest the benefits of AI.
Clear the Debris
While leaf litter and last year’s plant matter may be an acceptable ground cover over the winter, it must be cleared for fresh growth. Those born in the 20th century are not digital natives like Generation Z.
We have distinct memories of “old ways” and the expectations from using old tools. Take note of this in the soil of your mind. Are you burdened with moldy old ideas that weigh you down and close out new ideas? Give yourself a fresh start by clearing away any fears or stale ideas to make way for our collective future.
The takeaway is quite literally to “take away” your old ideas and clear out a space for planting the seeds and growing your relationship with AI.
Learn the Land
Whether or not you’re an active gardener, you may be familiar with the hardness zones of your local climate. Gardeners rely on these zones and information about their soil’s texture, acidity level, and nutrition. The zone chart is easy enough; it’s on the back of every seed package and wrapped around potted plants. However, how do gardeners learn about their soil?
Many gardeners engage with their local county extension offices, agricultural universities, community gardens, libraries, or retailers to get the necessary information. With the Internet, they can also find more resources from entities from the Department of Agriculture to webcast content.
Likewise, public libraries, community colleges, university extension programs, nonprofits, and software companies offer a mixture of free and low-cost educational opportunities about AI so you can grow to know what you don’t know in preparation for pursuing a personalized education plan.
The takeaway is to explore and embrace your community’s learning resources so you can find both the best information and learning styles to suit the kind of AI knowledge you want to build.
Amend and Fertilize
When the gardener knows both what they want to plant and the nature of their soil, they can add drainage and nutrients as needed to optimize their soil. Once you have done the work to understand what you want to pursue in your AI learning journey, you can collect the resources and tools necessary to initiate and accelerate your growth.
Arranging time in your calendar and setting milestones for your AI learning journey will give you the rich soil to sprout your ideas and learn how AI can benefit you and your life. Once you’ve done the proper planning and preparation, you can begin to grow into new opportunities.
The takeaway is to refine your plan and prepare the community resources and yourself for the AI work ahead.
Sowing and Growing
Gardeners know that there is a time in every season and don’t want to miss the moment. The hours of preparation will save weeks of perspiration, but that’s only an efficiency to make the process more effective. Even the best-planned garden will require hard work. The difference between a dedicated gardener and a reluctant one is that the dedicated individual finds the work enjoyable and focuses on the end result.
AI will only be more dominant and important, so checking out once you’ve started will leave you starved for information. Ideally, you assessed your plans and made your AI growing pattern fun by dedicating yourself to something about AI that interests you and that you found engaging learning methods.
So, once you start the ongoing learning journey, you can maintain consistency by investing yourself and your time into manageable time cycles. A forgotten garden is much more difficult to reclaim and requires more work than a tended garden.
The takeaway is to regularly recommit to your AI learning journey so that you can enjoy the benefits of your efforts.
Anticipate your First Harvest and Future Seasons
Have you ever had, or have you ever been, that neighbor or coworker who is desperately trying to give away all their extra zucchini or spends hours in late summer canning tomatoes because they grew more than they needed?
The nice thing about knowledge and skills is that you can share them in perpetuity, and they keep much fresher than produce. Nonperishable knowledge contributes to every subsequent season. The skills you learn by committing to your AI knowledge journey will benefit your family, friends, and coworkers.
The takeaway is to adopt the processes you apply to learn AI to continue your technical education in meaningful and personal ways throughout your life.

title: Council Post: Generative AI Is A Game Changer For Talent Transformation
text:
Prithvi Shergill, CEO of entomo.
Generative AI, the relentless disruptor across industries, continues to evoke exhilaration and promise with its capacity to effortlessly produce text and images, write or rectify code, make decisions and even fabricate complete virtual environments and has captured the world's imagination. Of course, its potential stretches far beyond these popularly acknowledged realms, and it's on the verge of transforming how we work and what skills we need to keep up with this innovative technology's disruption.
At the heart of businesses adapting to GenAI tools is talent transformation, which involves upskilling employees so they can assume new roles, adapt to emerging technologies and contribute to the creation of superior products. Having worked in the field of creating talent and human capital value, I see the unfathomable potential for generative AI in this area of HR function. Here are just a few ways this technology will be a game changer.
1. Enhancing Talent Acquisition
The traditional hiring process often involves a laborious cycle of reviewing résumés, conducting interviews and checking references. Generative AI can streamline this process by automating various tasks, like drafting job descriptions and personalizing candidate communications. AI-powered tools can then analyze vast amounts of data and define the most suitable candidate profile based on skills, experience and cultural fit. This reduces the time and effort required to screen applicants, allowing your recruiters to focus on more value-added tasks.
Another promising aspect is GenAI's ability to enable workforce planning. It can help your department set parameters for talent acquisition by predicting future talent needs.
2. Personalizing Learning And Growth Trajectories
Building employees' current or future skills and creating a high-performing workforce is a fundamental priority for any organization's growth. Generative AI tools offer significant advantages to enhance the quality and speed of upskilling by creating personalized learning experiences for individuals. By using AI to tailor learning and development, you can enhance employees' knowledge, skills, activities/abilities and task preferences. You can also use these tools to put together personalized growth trajectories, which encourage employees to stay with your organization so they can evolve at a pace that works for them.
3. Investing In Skill Health
Generative AI tools can make predictive analytics affordable and accessible at any time to users. These technologies can tap into company data, as well as information from the larger community, to provide insights into future skill demands and supply. This proactive foresight would allow your business to pinpoint talent segments that can fill potential skill gaps in your workforce.
Furthermore, in environments where investment needs to be made cautiously, a holistic view of the skill health of targeted talent is essential for directing where time, resources and effort will deliver a return on investment. GenAI can offer real-time decision support data as HR leaders look to source and/or staff talent, so they can make selections based on the skills of individuals across teams, companies and cities.
4. Making Talent Transformation Intelligent
One of generative AI's most significant implications is giving talent management professionals the ability to communicate information to executives and their board of directors. It helps leadership look around corners, rather than just in the rearview mirror, when shaping strategy or making decisions.
Using AI to connect the various elements influencing employee experience, such as job satisfaction, workload and employee sentiment, gives you access to actionable insight. For example, these analytics can identify employees who are at risk of leaving your organization by pinpointing early warning signals. At that point, you can take proactive, preventive measures to ensure you can retain valuable talent.
Additionally, AI-powered chatbots and virtual assistants can enhance the employee experience by providing round-the-clock support for routine HR inquiries, requests and policy information.
A Word Of Caution
Like any frontier technology, generative AI's potential impact on talent transformation should only be leveraged while ensuring ethical considerations in line with both company culture and national legislation. For example, without careful design and training, AI systems can inadvertently perpetuate historical biases, leading to unfair practices in talent acquisition and management. To mitigate this risk, it's imperative to uphold transparency and accountability. Regular auditing of AI algorithms and datasets is essential to identify and rectify bias. Additionally, diverse teams of data scientists and ethicists must be involved in a system's development and validation.
Privacy stands out as another major concern, particularly given AI systems' reliance on access to sensitive employee data. Companies must establish robust data protection and privacy policies to ensure the secure handling of this information. Prioritizing employee consent and data security is paramount when incorporating GenAI into talent transformation efforts.
The enterprise of tomorrow needs to recognize that ways of working successfully today won't lead to being future-ready. To engage, enable and empower individual and collective performance, organizations must step up to seed and nurture new ideas and initiatives. That's when proficiency and performance can be harvested and translated into value and growth.

title: Council Post: Digital Renaissance: AI And VR In The Gaming And Tech Industry
text:
Founder and CEO of Gameverse Interactive Corp, an industry-leading gaming company.
Artificial intelligence (AI) and virtual reality (VR) are sparking a renaissance in the gaming and tech industry. Advances in AI and VR are not just improving and changing the industry, it’s changing the way we play, and it’s creating a new wave of innovation and expansion that’s taking gaming to farther and more staggering levels than anyone ever thought possible.
AI’s Role In Gameplay
Artificial intelligence has been both, at best—a tool to create better gameplay and mechanics—and at worst—something that some players can use to gain unfair advantages over other players. With advanced enough artificial intelligence algorithms, you can create aimbots, or infer where certain players are through wallhacks and other nefarious methods. This can be problematic for developers trying to create fun and balanced multiplayer games. However, artificial intelligence also can help gamers to become exceptionally good at skill-based games with guidance, and insight. Learning algorithms can take information about the player and break it down into suggestions and training programs that can teach players to master games and even create better strategies. AI can provide real-time answers and aid to questions and can even provide tips and suggestions.
AI’s Impact On Game Development
The central paradigm shift I believe artificial intelligence is spurring in games is that it is changing the very fabric of game development itself. Developers are leveraging artificial intelligence to streamline, speed up and productivity boost the game development process by extending workflows while simultaneously cutting down debug times. By democratizing expertise, beginner-level developers are now able to compete on the same playing field as top-tier developers and usher in a new era of creativity and innovation. From procedural and generative content, allowing developers the ability to generate levels, textures and all kinds of special effects to create larger-than-life worlds that are more vibrant, realistic and dynamic than before.
Virtual Reality Enhanced By AI
Virtual reality is also getting a major makeover. AI-powered VR experiences offer unprecedented levels of engagement and immersion, for example, NPCs (non-playable characters) with complex behaviors and traits that dynamically adapt depending on their interactions with the environment and users. One of the most promising enhancements resulting from the integration of AI in VR environments is the ability to make our interactions with the virtual world and players more intuitive and natural, such as with gesture recognition, voice commands and other user interfaces, making the experience more immersive and engaging, which in turn can broaden the appeal of the game to more players.
Impact Beyond Gaming
The combinatorial effect of AI on VR is going to have far-reaching consequences, not just in terms of gaming alone. Virtual reality can be applied as a training aid that simulates real-life scenarios, and even transform the way education works by making subjects such as history and science more immersive to learn. Personalized learning experiences can be developed using AI to help students and developers master more complex skills in many different industries ranging from gaming to manufacturing. The emergence of AI and VR will transform the way people work by creating more immersive and more efficient simulation environments that help workers become better at their jobs and increase their rates of productivity and efficiency.
Challenges And The Road Ahead
The question of how artificial intelligence (AI) and virtual reality (VR) technologies will be used in gaming and technology must be addressed by gaming communities, technology leaders and educational institutions at every level. This includes appropriately managing issues related to fair play and maintaining an equal playing field for all users, as well as exploring how and if gamers are willing to give up certain identity information for immersive VR experiences. Moreover, education and gaming communities should ensure that the technology is user-friendly and is developed with accessibility and disability in mind so that no one gets left behind because of a lack of resources or accommodations required for a person with a physical or mental disability. It is also imperative to collaborate to reduce algorithmic bias that may result from the sophistication of the programming of AI-driven VR gaming and take further steps to diversify the development and design fields in the process.
The emerging field of immersive gaming and online interactions through VR must cultivate aspects of integration and interoperability and eventually promote not only robot-human interaction but also human-to-human communicative interactions that take place primarily through AI-enhanced VR.

title: Council Post: Generational Investment Trends And Automation In Modern Trading
text:
CEO, Co-Founder, 8081.
Investing has always been a dynamic endeavor, shaped by individual preferences, economic landscapes and technological advancements. Today, understanding generational investment trends is crucial for both investors and financial advisors. From millennials to baby boomers, each generation brings unique perspectives, goals and attitudes toward investing. Moreover, the advent of automation—driven by artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML)—has transformed the investment landscape, offering new opportunities and challenges.
Generational Investment Trends
Millennials: Known for their tech-savvy nature, millennials frequently opt for digital investment platforms and advisors due to their ease of use and accessibility. Many millennials, recognizing their longer investment horizon, are more open to assuming higher risks in pursuit of potentially greater returns. They exhibit a preference for growth-oriented investments and opportunities in emerging markets. Additionally, millennials are drawn to alternative assets beyond traditional stocks, showing a strong resonance with impact investing, which mirrors their inclination toward innovation and social change.
Generation X (Gen X): Generation X investors often prioritize wealth accumulation for retirement and other long-term financial goals. They seek stability and balance in their investment portfolios. Skeptical of traditional financial institutions, Generation X may explore alternative investment options such as peer-to-peer lending, real estate crowdfunding and private equity. Diversification across asset classes is important to Generation X, who often prefer a mix of stocks, bonds and real estate to mitigate risk and maximize returns. Income generation is a key consideration, leading many Generation X investors to favor dividend-paying stocks and fixed-income securities.
Baby Boomers: Baby boomers typically focus heavily on retirement planning and wealth preservation. Capital preservation and consistent income streams are paramount. They exhibit a more conservative investment approach, favoring blue-chip stocks, government bonds and annuities. Many baby boomers prioritize legacy planning and wealth transfer, incorporating estate planning strategies into their investment decisions. Longevity risk is a significant concern, prompting baby boomers to explore longevity insurance and other products designed to mitigate the financial impact of extended life expectancy.
Generation Z: Generation Z investors are entering the investment landscape with a focus on financial education and empowerment. They seek to understand investment fundamentals and explore diverse opportunities. As digital natives, Generation Z investors are comfortable with online investment platforms and mobile apps. They value simplicity, transparency and user-friendly interfaces. Innovation drives Generation Z investment preferences, with a keen interest in emerging technologies, disruptive industries and cryptocurrency. Environmental sustainability and social impact are central considerations for many Generation Z investors, influencing their investment decisions and portfolio allocations.
The Role Of Automation In Modern Trading
Automation has revolutionized investment trading, offering various options for automating trading activities, either through DIY methods or with guidance from a financial advisor. While some options are sophisticated, others are more user-friendly. In today's modern world, AI has become a cornerstone in analyzing the market and providing better insights.
However, despite promising results, automation and AI have limitations in adapting to unforeseen market events and shifts in sentiment. They heavily rely on preset algorithms that may overlook nuanced market behaviors. To overcome these limitations, businesses can combine automated trading with human oversight or integrate a hybrid approach using AI/ML technologies for more advanced analysis. This ensures flexibility in adjusting strategies to align with evolving market conditions and unforeseen events.
Artificial Intelligence (AI) And Machine Learning (ML)
In the trading realm, AI and ML help analyze past data, market trends and news sentiment to predict outcomes and guide investment choices. These advanced tools can offer users deeper insights into the market, enhancing understanding and performance. Sentiment analysis tools employ natural language processing (NLP) algorithms to assess market sentiment, allowing them to pinpoint potential trading opportunities or risks.
Risk Management And Portfolio Optimization
Automation can facilitate real-time risk management and portfolio optimization, helping investors mitigate downside risk and enhance portfolio performance. Portfolio rebalancing—similar to index trading but more as a DIY approach—ensures that asset allocations remain aligned with investors' risk preferences and investment objectives.
Investor Protection And Compliance
Automation can enhance investor protection and regulatory compliance by automating trade surveillance, fraud detection and anti-money laundering (AML) procedures. Robust compliance frameworks provide adherence to regulatory requirements and industry standards, safeguarding investors' interests and maintaining market integrity.
Understanding generational investment trends and the impact of automation in modern trading is crucial for effectively navigating today's financial markets. Financial advisors and investors must grasp these trends to navigate the complexities of the investment landscape. Each generation—from Gen Z to baby boomers—brings unique preferences, attitudes and priorities to their investment choices.
Moreover, automation, fueled by AI and ML technologies (or hybrid), can cater to the needs of different generations by reshaping their investment landscape, offering opportunities for efficiency, risk management and investor protection. By embracing automation and remaining aware of generational trends, investors can build robust portfolios that match their evolving requirements and aspirations in a constantly changing marketplace.

title: Council Post: Reengineering Enterprise Software With An AI-First Mindset
text:
Matt Berseth, co-founder and CIO of NLP Logix.
Artificial intelligence (AI) is transforming how businesses operate. While consumer-facing AI—like photo filters and virtual assistants—typically grabs the headlines, a large opportunity resides within enterprise software systems. Legacy enterprise software, often outdated and rigid, is now ready for an AI overhaul.
Over the past 30 years, there have been billions of lines of code written that power enterprise applications. These codebases are primarily implementing complex, rules-based software systems. Recent advances in AI, including large language models (LLMs) and generative AI (GenAI) in 2023, make AI-centric enterprise software upgrades essential. The software has always given businesses leverage, amplifying returns through efficiency gains. Enterprises must rebuild legacy software with an AI-first mindset to maintain this competitive edge. Those who can successfully blend advanced analytics, machine learning and generative AI throughout their software will be best set up for long-term success.
Modernizing enterprise software presents a prime opportunity to build systems oriented around AI capabilities from the ground up, rather than digitizing old ways of working. Even basic machine learning techniques like regression and tree-based models can drive significant efficiency gains relative to systems lacking predictive intelligence. By incorporating both cutting-edge generative AI and traditional machine learning methods into their software, enterprises can incrementally rebuild systems with expanding capabilities that create ongoing value.
The AI-transforming enterprise software shares core technologies with consumer AI applications, but its objectives, complexities and approach are very different. As businesses increasingly rely on AI, recognizing those differences is key for successfully deploying AI.
The Last Mile
AI’s "last mile" is where untapped potential lies for enterprises. While pretrained foundation models provide a strong basis, realizing value requires adapting and grounding these models to an organization's unique data assets and business challenges. This final stretch of integration and customization represents the key to converting AI's potential into software providing competitive differentiation.
Rather than treating AI models as turnkey black boxes, the firms gaining the most leverage are those digging into the details of model refinement and customization. By combining algorithms with internal datasets and clearly defined use cases, they can tune and optimize to deliver specialized AI capabilities not found in off-the-shelf solutions. As enterprises enter the last mile, adapting and enhancing their domain expertise and resources, they position themselves to extract maximum value.
Avoid Answers Without Context
For AI systems to be trusted, they must move beyond black box models to transparent and explainable AI. Leaders rightfully hesitate to act on recommendations from systems they cannot understand or audit. Without visibility into the reasoning and data behind predictions, there is no way to verify system reliability and prevent unintended harm from potential biases. As enterprises adopt increasingly powerful and complex AI, retaining contextual transparency is crucial.
By tracking and exposing the inference logic and relevant training data associated with each prediction, they enable stakeholders to understand the logic of system behaviors before taking action. Context visibility establishes justified trust and accountability. Understanding the strengths and limitations of the data and algorithms in play allows users to incorporate that context into adoption. The future success of enterprise AI hinges on retaining transparency as much as pursuing accuracy.
Staying Ahead Of The Curve
The age of AI is upon us, and it promises to reshape nearly every industry. Enterprises that embrace the "last mile" with customization and refinement and provide transparency to their systems will be adopted and deliver value. Those who choose not to adopt or take a wait-and-see approach will be left behind.

title: How Will Artificial Intelligence Impact Inequality And Energy?
text:
The rapid advance of technology and its impact on skilled and unskilled workers has hovered over the American landscape since the 2016 presidential election. For instance, the move to sustainable energies has displaced coal workers and changed the face of Appalachia.
The economic transition has disheartened many, allowing political opportunists to exploit the frustration. However, our leaders should encourage workers to adapt to markets — to build solar panels, wind turbines, and electric batteries. And now, Artificial Intelligence (AI) will hasten the changes, affecting every industry and every employee — especially those working in energy.
“One of our big challenges has always been workforce development and how to train the next generation of workers,” says Robert Austin, senior manager of EPRI — the research and development arm for utilities. “AI offers a real opportunity to learn new skills,” but we must “ease this transition.”
The United States Energy Association held a virtual press conference last week on AI in which Austin appeared, and I was among the journalists asking questions.
AI eliminates routine tasks so those running heavy industrial operations can solve problems and improve performance, which translates into healthier bottom lines. Energy companies can, therefore, gather data and test millions of outcomes before making a final judgment. Humans have limits.
For example, power plant and grid managers will have the tools to balance supply and demand and predict weather patterns, allowing them to accurately measure when wind and solar resources will be available.
Where In The World Is AI Headed?
According to McKinsey & Company, AI and digitization can increase asset productivity by up to 20% while reducing maintenance costs by 10%. The impact on the economy? PwC puts that at $15.7 trillion by 2030. China and North America will benefit the most, seeing their gross domestic products rise by double-digits in some communities. AI affects product enhancements, which stimulate demand and potential growth.
“AI lets us simulate a significant number of options and make recommendations for the best course of action,” says Marc Spieler, senior managing director for Nvidia. “You will always have humans in the loop orchestrating decisions. We will make better decisions using AI.”
The federal government granted $50 million to Portland General Electic, which leads a consortium with Utilidata and NVIDIA
The digital divide may widen. In the 1990s, I wrote about how the affluent had access to computers and the internet while disadvantaged communities did not. Today, the students focusing on science, technology, engineering, and mathematics have the upper hand — the critical knowledge supporting AI. They can afford tomorrow’s products, but what about everyone else?
If AI increases productivity, companies can increase profits. They can hire workers to help them meet demand. But those jobs will require more skills. While the technology will render some duties obsolete, it opens the door to many others. Workers must, therefore, stay on the cutting edge. For example, businesses are starting to hire chief AI officers.
"In the short term, we're going to see people utilizing artificial intelligence, replacing other people"—especially where repetitive tasks are involved, says David Derigiotis, chief insurance officer at Embroker Inc. “People must re-tool and up-level their knowledge. AI will change things. The implementation of technology has always had some ripple effect."
Undoubtedly, the world's most advanced economies will deploy AI tools. But will emerging countries have the same access? Consider the quest to hit net-zero targets, which requires money and technology: Carbon finance is probably the biggest hurdle to success—money that would go into the latest and greatest technologies that cut emissions and improve processes.
Clinton Vince, head of Dentons' U.S. Energy Practice, said that the digital divide between developed and developing nations is "very, very real." Take Sub-Saharan Africa: It is trying to electrify, and AI could help it place wind and solar farms and give its economies more momentum if it can overcome the barriers to entry.
The concern, of course, is that AI will worsen inequality — not just among workers but also among countries. Change is occurring at a more rapid rate than ever before. People can either choose to keep up or deny reality. Responsible leaders will explain that economic advancement is continuous and inevitable. Indeed, America was once an agricultural economy, and today, the digital age dominates — an era pushing us harder than ever before.

title: Are Expectations For Gen AI Lower Than Planned?
text:
I am coming to the conclusion that the hoped-for gen AI spending wave for both tech and tech services could be longer in developing than both the investors and companies are planning on. In a recent blog, I talked about the realization that most (perhaps as high as or above 90%) of the Proof of Concept (POC) initiatives that launched during 2023 will not make it to production in 2024. Yet, the tech firms are plowing hundreds of millions of dollars into building AI tools and building the capabilities for running them. What has changed? And where are there still opportunities for this important technology?
Change In Decision Makers
We at Everest Group partnered with Yates Ltd. and CalypsoAI and convened a panel of 50 CIOs and CTOs in Fortune 500 and other large enterprises for ongoing conversations about their gen AI journeys and how to invest in and leverage this fast-moving technology wisely.
It is evident that over the last few months there is a new set of stakeholders that entered the decision rights of who authorizes and funds Gen AI. And the question that they ask has changed.
The people added to the decision rights are departmental managers. I'm not talking about the head of business lines; I'm talking about managers and departments – the budget holders for those departments.
They are very practical. Instead of focusing on where AI can work, they want to know where AI is working. They ask questions such as “Where are people like me in other companies using it?” and “How specifically are they using it in my set of responsibilities?”
Where they are convinced that other people like themselves in large companies and with the same set of responsibilities are using gen AI for specific tasks, they are very open to funding and sponsoring the adoption of it for those tasks. They are not interested in further experiments on what the technology could do.
Furthermore, in making their decisions, there does not appear to be a lot of calculation around return on investment (ROI). The ROI appears to be inferred. (“If other people like me are using it for these tasks, then I will give serious consideration to also adopting it.”)
Pricing And Use Cases
Gen AI as currently priced is extremely expensive. This price appears to be starting to come down. I believe it will fall much further because soon there will be substantial efficiencies – not in computational power but in the use of the computational power to run gen AI engines. This will dramatically make use cases much more efficient.
If we look at potentially a 10X improvement in efficiency in the use of computational power for gen AI combined with only a small portion of the use cases being adopted, it is quite possible that we are looking at a significant over-capacity situation in the next six to nine months.
That over-capacity may be good for the consumer because that could well lead to significantly lower cost for the use of gen AI. But it is troubling or potentially troubling for both the tech firms and the tech services firms that count on the gen AI wave driving their next round of growth.
Current pricing for most gen AI tools is far too complicated for departmental managers to absorb. Pricing needs to be simplified to something that is much simpler to understand and predict than the usage-plus-token structure that often emerges in gen AI tools.
Pricing not only needs to be simpler but also needs to drop. I believe there is a strong likelihood that the pricing will drop in the short to medium future.
Implications Of Change In Decision Rights
As I explained above, decision rights for funding gen AI expanded to include departmental managers, and those managers are less inclined to think about where it could be used but, rather, where it is being used. They need clarity as to exactly which tasks it is applicable to in their set of responsibilities.
This change in the sentiment of the buying population has very significant implications for tech firms that are seeking to sell their products as well as tech services firms that seek to have the revenue for implementing and operating these products.
The first implication is the need for change in messaging. Today, the messaging around gen AI is focused on steering imagination on what it could do. The launch of widely or freely available ChatGPT sparked that attention, and it got industry and individuals thinking broadly around where it could be used.
Departmental managers no longer want to go through these sorts of experiences. They look for practical answers that they can use today. So, the messaging must bring it down to a level to show exactly what it will do, which tasks it enhances or eliminates, and which responsibilities are affected. The messaging also needs assurance that other companies and people like themselves are successfully succeeding.
The problem with this messaging is that there are countless departments with a specific task that gen AI can, in fact, be applied to and is being applied. So, the messaging is too complicated.
Another factor is that increasingly the adoption of gen AI is a business problem, not a technical problem. Yes, there are some technical issues involved and some security issues. But most of the issues are around integrating gen AI into new work.
This requires domain industry knowledge and domain experience as well as technical experience or technical skills, making this both a messaging and a channel nightmare for the existing tech messages and channels.
One potential answer is to use tech services allies to deliver that message at the departmental level in a concrete way. Use them as a channel that can communicate easily and tactically with the departmental managers around the specific tasks that their tools can impact and also help those departmental managers with the tasks of implementation, education and change management, which would increase business and consulting needs.
Hence, it appears that there needs to be much greater reliance on tech services firms to bring these tools to market.
Gen AI lacks the benefit that many historical technical implementations bring in a technology such as ERP or CRM. There is often a 4X increase in tech services spending over the cost of the tech. However, that does not seem to be happening in gen AI because the implementation and SI requirements are not that heavy.
That said, there seems to be an open door for multidisciplinary teams or consulting needs to help the business understand and start using the tools. So, the nature of the opportunity for the tech services firms appears to be substantially different from the ones that they experienced with ERP or CRM or other similar technologies.
Where Are The Opportunities in 2024?
Gen AI is a very important technology that will have significant benefits for individuals and businesses. And some of those benefits will start showing up in 2024.
It appears that the most used for enterprises currently is in feature or product extensions for already-existing platforms. For example, gen AI tools that make the sales operations platform with all the sales data better appear to be getting traction, likewise, for the marketing stack, where some traction is occurring.
This pattern goes on where a company already has a tech stack with a significant pool of data that the gen AI tool can then be laid over and provide a feature or product extension for that set of technology that is already in existence.
In other words, gen AI looks like to be a highly complementary technology for existing digital platforms. This is where we see substantial trust.
An example is Microsoft Copilot. The data already exists in the Microsoft Office platform, and Microsoft Copilot is a feature extension of that platform. It adds additional value or additional usefulness. The tool makes that platform work better.
There are still plenty of those opportunities. Most companies will have a number of opportunities to deploy gen AI productively, even using the high standard of only using tools that are already in production by people in other companies in their same situation.
When we look outside of those situations, there seems to be a much longer adoption cycle, and it is unclear when widescale adoption will occur elsewhere.

title: How Financial Services Firms Can Unleash The Power Of Generative AI
text:
Banks and insurers have built-in hype detectors and pride themselves on their ability to differentiate between fads and genuine value-adding innovation. Over the past 15 months, their antennae have been tested as never before by the unrestrained fervor surrounding generative AI.
Consider this: since OpenAI unleashed ChatGPT in November 2022, we have tracked the launch of a further 623 foundation models that either address a specific business use case or provide a generic tool for tasks such as code testing. Meanwhile, the FinTech Innovation Lab New York, a fintech accelerator program that offers mentorship and advice from leading financial services firms, including JPMorgan Chase, BlackRock and Prudential, among others, is close to finalizing its next cohort. Ninety percent of the finalists – which are selected directly by the FS institutions – are focused on generative AI solutions.
One of the tests to distinguish between fool’s gold and the real deal is ‘show me the money’. There’s no shortage of that, from Microsoft’s investment of $13 billion in OpenAI and Meta’s announcement of its $33 billion commitment to the technology, to the recent news that SoftBank's Masayoshi Son and OpenAI’s Sam Altman are both hoping to raise huge amounts – $100 billion and up to $7 trillion respectively – to accelerate the production of AI chips. If that sounds excessive – global computer chip sales last year amounted to a little over $500 billion.
Generative AI really is different from most of the major technological innovations the world has seen to date – could even the internet claim to have changed virtually every part of every business? Add to this universality the staggering pace at which the technology is advancing and diversifying, and even the greatest skeptic has to admit that we are witnessing an exceptional phenomenon.
Most financial services professionals agree. Throughout 2023, virtually every financial firm worked on identifying use cases and running proofs of concept. 2024 should be the year when they shift from experimental mode to the systematic, cross-enterprise pursuit of value.
There’s a lot more to this than just shifting gears and ramping up investment. To unlock the full value of generative AI, banks, insurers and capital markets firms will need to examine the fundamentals of their business. Most will have to upgrade their digital core because the technology cannot fire on all cylinders if the company doesn’t have a flexible IT architecture based on cloud and a modern data foundation.
All will need to rethink what work will be required and how it will be performed, and the impact of this on skills, roles and the organization itself. Given the pace and extent of change, traditionally conservative firms will have to radically transform their culture to become more fluid, adaptive and innovative. Their leaders will need a solid understanding of the potential of AI if they are to continue to influence the direction and evolution of their organizations.
These firms will have to bring their workers along for the journey and many will be uneasy. In a study we carried out late last year, we found that only 31% of financial services firms have comprehensive strategies in place to ensure positive worker outcomes and experiences with generative AI.
The reality is that if you succeed at capturing the full potential of generative AI you will, by definition, have reinvented your business. Few are ready for this. Workers are eager to be trained in generative AI, but not many financial services employers are truly meeting this demand.
This, of course, is good news for the front-runners, but all is not lost for those falling behind. The democratization of generative AI technology makes it easier for firms to catch up, provided they make the right strategic choices.
We all enjoyed playing with ChatGPT when it first came out, posing improbable challenges and marveling at its ability to swiftly deliver impressive responses. Implementing the technology to transform your operating model, customer experience and workforce is an altogether more demanding proposition. It demands a systematic strategy that reaches into every part of the value chain and a multi-year program that enables continuous reinvention.
A crucial part of this strategy is selecting from a growing array of increasingly sophisticated – and increasingly specialized – AI models. We talk about the need for a ‘model garden’ which allows you to nurture, try out and capitalize on a variety of models for different purposes. Another is understanding the vital role of the cloud. This includes provision of the necessary compute power, as well as making your data securely accessible to your preferred models.
There’s also no getting away from the fact that a great deal of preparatory work will be needed by most companies. Ultimately, if your data is not organized and secure, you can’t expect to make full use of it. If your culture doesn’t encourage curiosity and experimentation, you will always trail the industry leaders. If your people don’t have the necessary skills and willingness to change, you’ll struggle to scale the technology throughout the organization. And if you haven’t considered proper guardrails and responsible AI, you’re likely to risk introducing bias and losing the confidence of your customers.
The excitement around generative AI is palpable. Seldom have we faced a future where so many of the pipe dreams of today are likely to become tomorrow’s reality. However, the full value of this innovation won’t be realized if financial services firms don’t first put in place the essential building blocks.

title: Council Post: Digital Tutors: Examining AI's Long-Term Impact On Language Education
text:
Dmitry Basalkin is the CEO and Founder of Bright Apps, which facilitates the mastery of languages through generative AI breakthroughs.
AI is transforming the world. However, not as fast as we expected when the attention on GPT and generative AI first skyrocketed. After the initial boom, in many respects, we've seen minimal changes in our daily personal and business lives.
But there is a huge market that is quickly becoming a playground for building and testing AI solutions: foreign language learning. As someone leading a company that uses AI to help empower language learning, I believe this area of education is capable of drastically changing the lives of millions of people.
Let’s see in detail examples of how those in the industry can apply recent advancements in AI technologies to foreign language learning, as well as what we can look forward to as the technology progresses.
Toward Digital Tutors
It is estimated that around two billion people are learning foreign languages. Individuals and companies spent $56 billion on language learning in 2022, which is projected to grow to $120 billion by 2030.
A growing number of AI-powered use cases in language learning mobile apps and strong interest from governments in applying AI for public education are already here.
A digital tutor for language learning cannot simply be another language learning model (LLM) like GPT4 nor a simple combination of prompts and AI assistants based on this model. To build a truly useful digital tutor, I believe we will need much more—a digital environment where each interaction feeds the learning loop for both the learner and AI agents who are working with the learner's personal history.
This includes multiple user interfaces, multiple AI models, the full story of interactions for each user, domain knowledge and skills structure, trusted sources of information for AI agents and many more facets.
Technologies necessary to develop effective digital tutors are already here. With recent advancements in speech recognition and voice generation, generative AI can now hear and speak as well as humans in many languages.
I am certain that we will see the first full implementation before 2024 ends. Of course, integration with national curriculum and pilot projects in schools will take a bit more time. I expect we will see millions of adults and children using digital tutors daily for language learning by next year.
Overcoming Hurdles
The cost of running LLMs necessary for digital tutors should decrease over time as new infrastructure and software become available. Some basic AI functions will be available to perform on mobile devices and effectively will be free. Based on my estimates, calculated from the average tutor's rate per hour, I expect to see the average cost of digital tutors to become 100 times cheaper when compared to one-to-one lessons with a human tutor in the next few years.
Digital tutors promise to offer personalized learning experiences to a vast number of students simultaneously, adapting to each learner's pace, style and needs. They can be accessible 24/7, removing the constraints of time and location. They can also process and analyze large amounts of data to provide instant feedback and tailor learning paths effectively.
Will teachers in schools be replaced with digital tutors? Not in the near future. I think the first goal should be to supplement the existing educational process and provide service in regions with a shortage of human teachers. As for tutors for adults and self-learning tools—they will need to master ways to implement digital tutors into their services or face falling behind the industry.
Wise governments as well can play a significant role in developing national programs to apply AI in public education and get advantages of these new technologies for their people. I see digital tutors as helping democratize quality education and contribute to a fair distribution of knowledge and opportunities in life.

title: Council Post: How Customer Support Agents Can Benefit From AI-Powered Software
text:
Tamas Ham-Szabo is the CEO of SAAS First, an AI and data-driven help desk for online businesses.
In my experience, AI has an undeniable impact on how customer service agents perform their daily tasks, considering a reduced workload, less dissatisfied and frustrated customers, improved options for customers to find solutions for their problems on their own and detailed and easily accessible insights on customer data.
So, let’s talk about how AI, in my experience working with companies using it in their operations, impacts the everyday lives of customer service agents.
Reducing Workload With Automation And Chatbot Implementation
Customer support agents have to deal with hundreds of cases a day, questions and issues coming one after the other, which can be very overwhelming. Naturally, the aim is to reduce this workload, which can be done through introducing automation and an AI chatbot service. Research by Hubspot explains that customer support specialists who use generative AI to create responses for customer queries save two hours and 11 minutes a day.
An AI chatbot can handle incoming queries with basic questions or issues that can be resolved easily. In my experience, the bigger the knowledge base that the chatbot is provided with, the better and more extensive answers it can give to customers' questions. Once the chatbot resolves these basic queries, the agents have less work to do, or they can even completely neglect to spend much time on these, as everything is automated. Thus, the workload on agents gets smaller.
Improved Availability Of Support
One of the biggest advantages of an AI chatbot is that it is there 24/7. Customers can have questions late at night, coming from different time zones or from companies that have different working hours. In these times, customer support agents might not be available. In my opinion, AI chatbots have a very significant role in answering queries immediately, which is a great feature from the agents’ point of view.
Even if the issue cannot be resolved immediately by the AI chatbot, it can give instant feedback to the customer that their issue is being handled. By that, when the agents get to the issue, they are faced with a customer who anticipates that it will take some time to resolve the problem.
Language Translations Overcoming Barriers
Language can be quite an intricate thing in customer service communications. Especially if the participants don’t speak the same language fluently. Using a translator can be a solution to such problems, however, those tools might not provide as accurately drafted messages, leaving some space for expressing the true and real stance of the customers. In addition, the agents might translate the message to understand it better but will give the answer in their spoken language, which can break the flow of the conversation and leave the personalization aspect neglected.
An AI chatbot can be used to understand the customer in their given language and craft responses specifically in that particular language. Hence, customer agents don’t need to worry about the translation or being unable to understand customers perfectly, leaving no space for errors during the communication process and saving them significant time.
Improved Self-Service Options And Reduced Issues
Another important aspect to consider for AI-powered customer service is that it can significantly boost the options for self-service. In fact, 67% of customers would go for a form of self-service instead of talking to a customer service representative.
In a business, it’s always a good strategy to create an environment where customers can find answers to their questions on their own. Such practices eliminate the need to contact support agents and potentially wait for their answers.
This is obviously in the support agent’s best interest because fewer people will reach out to them with routine questions and basic troubleshooting. Their time can be dedicated to more challenging and complex problems, which will save time, plus it’s also more intellectually stimulating, leading to more fulfillment in their job.
Refined Customer Insights Used For Better Understanding
AI can be used to carry out detailed and very intricate analytics based on vast amounts of data from different touchpoints. That is a great way for support agents to better understand customer behaviors, preferences and patterns.
With detailed insights into what customers do and what they like, agents have the opportunity to offer personalized help, recommendations, or solutions. This makes the agents’ job easier to create conversations with customers that are unique and valuable each time.
What is more, AI-driven analytics can also tell you a lot about potential risks, such as potential churn or experienced dissatisfaction. When the agent is provided with such information, it becomes much simpler for them to proactively approach these people and, with that, increase customer retention and satisfaction.
Implementing AI Chatbots
To get started with the implementation of an AI chatbot, the first advice I could give you is to check any advancements in AI. This kind of technology is evolving faster than any other we’ve experienced in the past. It’s best if you see whether your desired solution already exists before you start implementing your own.
With that being said, you also have to consider that there are limited educational resources about the implementation of AI into a business. In addition, these sources are always changing due to the fast-evolving nature of the technology. The number of experts in the field of AI implementation and prompt engineering is very limited, and they are usually already engaged in a project.
Another thing you need to recognize is that AI is not exact. What I mean by this is that creating a working, quality application takes a lot of time. You need to calculate longer developments and testing cycles than usual. This is also usually influenced by changes in the AI department. If you think about it, just OpenAI alone launched numerous new models and solutions in the last year. So, it can be quite difficult to keep yourself up to date with the latest technologies and developments.
Conclusion
AI tools make the job of customer support agents more manageable and smoother. They help by taking care of simple questions, being available all the time, breaking language barriers, letting customers help themselves and understanding customer needs better. All of these contribute to the agents’ work being less stressful and more rewarding.

title: Council Post: 2024 Is The Year Of AI, But Data Will Steal The Show
text:
Afif Khoury, CEO of SOCi, has forged a career spanning over 25 years at the forefront of technology and data-driven innovation.
As we settle into the promising realm of 2024, artificial intelligence (AI) is poised to deliver even more groundbreaking transformations that will redefine how businesses operate, innovate and leverage information. Already, we’re witnessing AI-driven advancements in predictive analytics that enhance decision-making processes and AI integration in customer service with sophisticated chatbots, providing seamless user experiences. These innovations are just the beginning of a broader trend where AI is not only automating tasks but also offering deeper insights and more personalized interactions.
While the AI revolution is real, promising significant changes in various industries, the transformation will unfold in stages—much like the digital, social and mobile eras. Given your use of AI is only as good as the breadth, quality and security of your data, the initial impact of AI will be most evident in the first wave of technologies affecting how organizations collect, ingest, analyze and secure data.
This coming year is set to witness a convergence of technologies and methodologies that will shape the data-driven future we've all been anticipating, specifically in the areas of data sourcing and preparation, data analysis and data security. Below are my top data trends for 2024 that will transform how we leverage data and prepare for an AI-dominated future.
Data Sourcing And Preparation
1. Intelligent Automation In Data Aggregation
In 2024, the data landscape will witness a paradigm shift toward aggregation. Disparate datasets in fragmented systems will give way to platform-aggregated datasets architected for AI analytics. Advanced machine learning algorithms will play a pivotal role in automating the aggregation process, allowing businesses to sift through vast and diverse datasets with unprecedented speed and accuracy. This automation will not only ensure efficiency but also enable organizations to derive actionable insights from the aggregated data.
2. The Emergence Of Data Marketplaces
Supplementing the trends in organizations' own data will be the rise of data marketplaces. The collaborative spirit of the digital age will lead platforms to facilitate the exchange of data between organizations, unlocking new possibilities for innovation and collaboration.
We'll explore how data marketplaces contribute to an interconnected and dynamic ecosystem, enabling businesses to access diverse datasets for informed decision-making. For example, brands may use marketplaces to marry data from their marketing platforms with lead data from CRMs, revenue data from point-of-sale systems and loyalty data from experience platforms to generate a 360-degree view of consumers’ journeys.
3. Augmented Data Management
Augmented analytics will elevate data management to new heights in 2024. Machine learning algorithms will automate data preparation, cleansing and integration processes, allowing data professionals to focus on strategic analysis. This trend streamlines workflows, minimizes errors and empowers organizations to extract meaningful insights from their data.
Data Analysis
1. AI-Infused Analytics: The Rise Of Augmented Intelligence
We will see a seamless integration of AI into analytics, giving birth to augmented intelligence. AI will enhance human decision-making processes, providing deeper insights and uncovering patterns that might have otherwise gone unnoticed. As businesses harness the power of AI-driven analytics, we can expect more accurate predictions, enhanced personalization and a significant leap in operational efficiency.
2. Data Democratization: Empowering The Non-Technical User
Data democratization will gather momentum as tools and platforms that empower non-technical users to access and understand data will become widespread. For example, busy store owners may begin to get easy-to-understand analytics about their marketing campaigns or digestible, previously buried sales trends data. This shift aims to make data-driven insights accessible to a broader audience within organizations, fostering a culture of informed decision-making at all levels.
3. Edge Computing: Processing Data At The Source
Edge computing will become mainstream, revolutionizing how data is processed and analyzed. By moving computing closer to the data source, or better yet, in the cloud, organizations can achieve real-time insights, reduced latency and improved security. Beyond software, as the Internet of Things (IoT) continues to grow, edge computing will prove instrumental in handling the massive influx of data generated by connected devices.
Data Security
1. Data Privacy And Ethics Taking Center Stage
With the increasing importance of data, the focus on privacy and ethics is more crucial than ever. Consumers are demanding greater transparency and control over their data. In response, businesses will be compelled to adopt robust privacy measures, ensuring ethical data practices.
We’ve already seen the beginning of these controls with examples like the European Union's General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR), which mandates businesses to protect the personal data and privacy of EU citizens by requiring explicit consent for data collection and providing rights for data access and erasure.
Similarly, California's Consumer Privacy Act (CCPA) gives residents the right to know what personal data is collected, to refuse the sale of their data and to have it deleted, compelling businesses to adopt stringent privacy measures. Moving forward, privacy-enhancing technologies and frameworks will become key components of data strategies to build and maintain trust in an interconnected world.
2. Blockchain Resurgence In Data Security
As concerns around data security persist, blockchain technology is set to make a resurgence. The decentralized and tamper-proof nature of blockchain offers a robust solution for securing sensitive data. For example, we are already seeing the healthcare industry adopting blockchain technology to secure patient medical records, ensuring data integrity and confidentiality.
By utilizing blockchain's decentralized, tamper-proof system, medical institutions can efficiently manage sensitive patient data while safeguarding against unauthorized access and data breaches. This shift promises enhanced security and privacy in handling health records across healthcare providers. You can expect to see increased adoption of blockchain in data management, ensuring the integrity and security of information across various industries.
As we navigate the dynamic landscape of data in 2024, these trends underscore the evolving nature of our data-driven world—and the limitless opportunities it presents. Embracing these shifts positions businesses on the cutting edge of innovation and empowers individuals with the knowledge to harness the full potential of data. It’s time to embark on this transformative journey and unlock the next chapter in the data revolution.

title: Council Post: AI In Incident Management: A Privacy-Centric Approach
text:
JJ Tang is the CEO and Co-founder of Rootly, an enterprise-grade incident management platform.
Imagine an alien, fluent in your language, silently joining your family discussions during a conflict. Its presence, although silent and unobtrusive, is keenly felt as it learns from the intimate details shared. This analogy reflects the current landscape of large language models (LLMs) like OpenAI's GPT, which understand and process human language, offering useful insights in an accessible format. Although LLMs are transforming our work environment by reducing daily cognitive loads, their deployment demands careful consideration of privacy and the necessity of an opt-out mechanism.
My team at Rootly embraced this challenge head-on when integrating AI capabilities into our Slack-based incident management solution. Given our product's role in customer infrastructure—managing outages, performance issues and bugs—privacy and compliance were our primary design considerations. This piece aims to convey the lessons learned from developing an AI solution with user privacy in mind.
The Enterprise Privacy Challenge
Privacy concerns aren't new. Instead, they've evolved from fears of totalitarian surveillance in the 20th century to the modern threats posed by social media to global democracies. Privacy concerns go beyond the fear of exposure; they highlight how the knowledge of being observed can fundamentally change behavior.
This phenomenon isn't limited to personal life. In the corporate world, attempts to track and improve developer productivity often lead to unintended consequences. Developers, aware of the metrics being used to judge their performance, may game the system to their advantage, undermining the very goal of the assessment.
Privacy extends into the realm of data management, encompassing how data is stored, processed and shared, with broad implications for legal compliance, security and corporate governance. When incorporating AI technologies, it's imperative that their privacy standards align with your organizational policies.
AI, Incident Management And Privacy
The impact of AI in incident management can be huge. AI can consolidate diverse data streams—the team’s findings, error traces or cluster metrics—enabling people to quickly understand and address issues. AI's capacity to digest complex datasets and offer actionable insights, suggest resolutions and even draft post-incident retrospectives is opening a new horizon in the industry.
Yet, the sensitive nature of such data necessitates a cautious approach. Incidents can be so sensitive that you want to classify them as private, such that not even your engineers know they exist. Thus, the integration of AI into these processes poses unique privacy challenges. Employing AI models involves sharing data with external parties for processing, raising valid concerns about data privacy and control.
Committing To Privacy By Design
Acknowledging that privacy requirements vary widely across industries and regulatory environments, it's essential to design an AI solution that makes customers confident about how their data is used. Based on feedback from users and industry research, we built a privacy framework that lets customers determine which incidents and specific Slack messages are subjected to AI analysis.
Additionally, given that incidents happen under pressure, there are inherent risks associated with handling sensitive production data. Thus, as a safety net, it's important to scrub personally identifiable information (PII), service secrets and other sensitive details before data is sent for AI processing.
Navigating The Shared Knowledge Landscape
LLMs accumulate and refine their knowledge base from vast databases, adjusting responses based on user input. Although improving an AI model's performance through data and feedback is beneficial, there's a legitimate concern about inadvertently aiding competitors with your proprietary data.
To address this, you'll want to partner with your LLM provider to ensure that customer data is neither stored nor utilized for training. For additional control and peace of mind, you can also consider offering customers the option to integrate their own LLM accounts, such as OpenAI.
Emphasizing User Control And Choice
The metaphor of the alien observer underscores the utility and potential discomfort of AI in personal spaces. Similarly, in the professional realm, the ability to opt in or out of AI features at will is crucial for maintaining operational flexibility without compromising privacy.
Incorporating AI into your operational toolkit shouldn't come at the expense of privacy. By choosing partners that prioritize these values, organizations can leverage AI to enhance their incident management processes while safeguarding the privacy and trust of their users.

title: AI & The Sinister Art Of Digital Grooming: A Call For Awareness & Action
text:
In the ever-evolving digital age, artificial intelligence (AI) has opened a Pandora's box of possibilities, not all of which are for social good. Among the darker uses of AI is the exploitation by sexual abusers to groom potential victims. This insidious use of technology is a stark reminder of the dual-edged nature of AI and the need for vigilant monitoring and ethical guidelines.
The Dark Turn of AI in Digital Grooming
Sexual predators have twisted AI's ability to analyze, learn, and interact to identify and groom potential victims, particularly in online spaces frequented by minors. This misuse involves a range of tactics, from creating realistic AI-driven avatars to deploying chatbots that engage and manipulate vulnerable individuals. To begin with, bad actors have corrupted AI avatars into a tool for deception. Through the creation of lifelike avatars, predators tailor these digital personas to appear as peers to the targeted individuals, breaking down barriers and gaining trust. The avatars, powered by sophisticated AI algorithms, conduct conversations that are convincingly human, making it difficult for victims, especially children and teenagers, to recognize the deception.
Likewise, bad actors have warped chatbots and AI algorithms into invisible predators. The groomers leverage these chatbots, designed to mimic human conversation patterns, to interact with potential victims on social media, gaming platforms, and chat rooms. The AI behind these bots analyzes victim responses and tailors future interactions to manipulate and groom victims subtly.
Because of the hidden nature of these activities, direct public examples of AI used for grooming by sexual predators are scarce, However, there have been instances where technology's role in such cases has come to light. For example, in online gaming platforms and chat rooms, there have been reports of predators using AI tools to engage with and groom young players. These cases often go undetected until it's too late, as the AI-driven interactions can be incredibly subtle and sophisticated.
The Implications of AI-Enabled Grooming
AI use in grooming has far-reaching implications, both for the victims and for society at large. This form of abuse leaves deep psychological scars, leading to long-term trauma and other mental health issues. Furthermore, the increasing sophistication of AI-driven grooming tools makes it challenging to detect and prevent these activities, posing a significant threat to online safety, especially for younger internet users. As a result, there is s massive erosion of trust in digital platforms, particularly those frequented by children and teenagers. It raises questions about the safety and security measures in place and the ethical responsibilities of platform providers to protect their users.
Then, AI use for grooming also presents a complex set of legal and ethical challenges. Laws and regulations struggle to keep pace with technological advancements, making it problematic to combat and prosecute such crimes effectively. There is also an ethical dilemma regarding the development and deployment of AI technologies, emphasizing the need for ethical AI development and usage guidelines.
Combating AI-Enabled Sexual Grooming
Addressing the misuse of AI in grooming requires a multi-pronged approach involving technology companies, law enforcement, policymakers, and the public. First, there is an urgent need to strengthen laws and regulations to address the specific challenges posed by AI-enabled grooming. This includes updating legal frameworks to cover the nuances of digital abuse and ensuring that law enforcement agencies are equipped with the necessary tools and knowledge to combat these crimes. Second, tech companies and AI developers must prioritize ethical considerations in the development and deployment of AI. This includes implementing strict guidelines to prevent the misuse of AI technologies and conducting thorough risk assessments to identify potential areas of abuse. Third, enhanced monitoring and detection mechanisms are crucial in the fight against AI-enabled grooming. Digital platforms need to employ advanced AI algorithms to detect suspicious behavior and interactions, coupled with human oversight to ensure accuracy and sensitivity in these matters. Fourth, raising public awareness about the risks and signs of AI-enabled grooming is essential. Educating parents, teachers, and young Internet users about online safety, the potential risks of interacting with strangers online, and the sophisticated nature of AI-driven interactions can help in early detection and prevention. Fifth, collaboration and information sharing among technology companies, law enforcement, and child protection agencies are vital. By sharing knowledge, resources, and best practices, these entities can work together more effectively to combat AI-enabled grooming.
Sadly, the growing misuse of AI for grooming by sexual predators is a disturbing reality of our digital age. It underscores the critical need for ethical AI development, stringent regulations, enhanced monitoring, and public awareness. As technology continues to advance, it is imperative that we remain vigilant and proactive in safeguarding the most vulnerable members of our society. The fight against AI-enabled grooming is not just a technological battle; it's a moral imperative that calls for collective action and responsibility.
